faqs.q: How many dealers can I have on Starter?
faqs.a: Twenty-five basic records. If you run a real channel, Professional makes them unlimited and adds the hierarchy and the portal, which is where the value actually is.

faqs.q: What can a dealer do in the portal?
faqs.a: Place orders against their agreed pricing, track order and dispatch status, download invoices and see their outstanding balance. They cannot see other dealers or your direct customers.

faqs.q: Can dealers have different prices?
faqs.a: Yes. Agreed pricing or a discount structure sits on the partner record and applies automatically to their orders.

faqs.q: Do dealer orders go through the same workflow?
faqs.a: Yes — same order, dispatch and invoice flow, with the dealer as the billing party. Channel business is not a parallel system with its own rules.

faqs.q: Is there deal registration?
faqs.a: No. We do not have a lead registration or MDF workflow. If channel conflict management is your main requirement, we are honest that this is not built for it yet.

items.name: Call hub and dialer
items.metaDescription: Dial from the customer record, log every call automatically, and keep recordings against the account. Live in KanchanFlow on every tier.
items.lead: Click to call from the record, and the call logs itself. No post-call data entry, no calls that happened but were never written down.
items.answer: The KanchanFlow call hub dials from inside the customer, quote or order record and logs every call automatically against it, with recording where you have enabled it. Because the RFQ-to-Order CRM holds the call next to the quote it concerns, the follow-up history is complete without anyone doing post-call data entry.
summary: The gap in every CRM is the call that happened but was never logged. Not because people are lazy, but because logging it is a second job after the conversation ended, and the next call is already ringing. The fix is to make the call itself the thing that creates the record.

Dial from inside a record and the call is logged with the contact, the duration, the outcome you pick from a short list, and the recording where enabled. Inbound calls from known numbers pop the customer record so the person answering already knows what is open with that account. Nobody has to ask a caller to hold while they find the file.

capabilities.title: Click to call from any record
capabilities.body: Dial from the customer, contact, quote or order. The call is associated with that record from the start rather than being reconciled afterwards.

capabilities.title: Automatic call logging
capabilities.body: Direction, duration, contact and timestamp are captured without typing. You add an outcome and a one-line note, which takes seconds rather than minutes.

capabilities.title: Recording against the account
capabilities.body: Where you have enabled recording and have consent, the recording is stored against the call on the customer record and is playable from there.

capabilities.title: Inbound screen pop
capabilities.body: A call from a known number opens the customer with their open quotes and outstanding balance, so whoever picks up is not asking who is calling.

capabilities.title: Call history on the timeline
capabilities.body: Calls, WhatsApp messages, emails and visits sit on one customer timeline in order. That timeline is what a handover between salespeople actually needs.

howItWorks.name: Connect your telephony
howItWorks.text: Link your calling provider to the workspace and assign numbers to users. Recording is configured here, including whether it is on by default.

howItWorks.name: Dial from the record
howItWorks.text: Open the customer or quote and press call. The contact and the record context are attached to the call before it connects.

howItWorks.name: Talk
howItWorks.text: The call runs through your provider. Duration and direction are captured automatically; nothing about the conversation depends on remembering to press a button.

howItWorks.name: Pick an outcome
howItWorks.text: After the call, select an outcome — quote discussed, revision requested, callback scheduled — and add a note. That takes about ten seconds.

howItWorks.name: Find it later
howItWorks.text: The call, the note and the recording sit on the customer timeline next to the quote it concerned, which is where the next person will look.

faqs.q: Do I need a separate phone system?
faqs.a: You need a telephony provider to carry the calls. We connect to it, dial from the record and log the result; we are not the carrier.

faqs.q: Is recording on by default?
faqs.a: No. Recording is configured by you, per workspace, and consent requirements vary by state and country. That decision should be deliberate.

faqs.q: Where are recordings stored?
faqs.a: Against the call on the customer record, counting against your workspace storage — 10 GB on Starter, 100 GB on Professional, 500 GB or more on Enterprise.

faqs.q: Does an inbound call find the right record?
faqs.a: If the number is known, yes — the customer opens with their open quotes and balance. Unknown numbers log as an unmatched call you can attach afterwards.

faqs.q: Can I see call activity by salesperson?
faqs.a: Yes, calls made, connected and their outcomes report by user. It is a coverage measure, not a surveillance tool, and we would not build the latter.

items.name: RFQ management
items.metaDescription: Makes the RFQ its own record with parts, drawings, due dates and a win-loss outcome, instead of an email thread. In development, target Wave 1 M2.
items.lead: Today an enquiry becomes a quote and the enquiry itself disappears. We are making the RFQ a record in its own right, with its own due date, its own owner and its own outcome.
items.answer: RFQ management makes the request for quote a first-class object in the KanchanFlow RFQ-to-Order CRM, separate from the quote that answers it. It is in active development at roughly 5 percent, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 2, and it is the record every other Wave 1 RFQ feature is being built on top of.
summary: Right now an enquiry turns into a quote and the enquiry stops existing. That is fine until you want to know your quote-to-RFQ ratio, how many RFQs you declined and why, or how long it takes your desk to turn an enquiry around. None of those questions can be answered from a list of quotes.

The work in progress makes the RFQ its own record: received date, source, buyer, the parts requested, the drawings supplied, the customer's required response date, an owner and an outcome. A quote is then something raised against an RFQ, and an RFQ can be declined without a quote ever existing, which is a legitimate and common answer.

capabilities.title: The RFQ as its own record
capabilities.body: Received date, source, buyer contact, required response date, owner and status live on the RFQ itself, not on a quote raised later.

capabilities.title: No-quote as a real outcome
capabilities.body: Declining an RFQ is a recorded decision with a reason — capacity, material, lead time, price expectation. Today that decision leaves no trace at all.

capabilities.title: Response-time measurement
capabilities.body: Time from RFQ received to quote sent, measured per estimator and per customer. This is the number most shops guess at and most buyers judge you on.

capabilities.title: Multiple quotes against one RFQ
capabilities.body: A complex enquiry may be answered with alternate approaches. Each is a quote against the same RFQ rather than three unconnected documents.

capabilities.title: Drawings attached to the RFQ
capabilities.body: The prints the customer supplied belong to the enquiry, not to the quote. They stay with the RFQ and are inherited by every quote raised against it.

howItWorks.name: The RFQ is created
howItWorks.text: From an email through AI extraction, from an IndiaMART enquiry, from a WhatsApp message or by hand. Source is recorded because response expectations differ by channel.

howItWorks.name: Parts and drawings are attached
howItWorks.text: Each requested part becomes a line on the RFQ with quantity and required date, and the supplied prints attach to the enquiry itself.

howItWorks.name: It is qualified and owned
howItWorks.text: An owner is assigned and the RFQ is qualified — do we make this, do we have capacity, is the required date possible. The answer may be no.

howItWorks.name: A quote is raised against it
howItWorks.text: One or more quotes reference the RFQ. Lines, drawings and dates carry across, and the RFQ shows what has been quoted and what has not.

howItWorks.name: The outcome is recorded
howItWorks.text: Won, lost or no-quote, with a reason. That is what turns a pile of enquiries into a win-rate you can act on.

tierAvailability.starter: Unlimited RFQ line items, unlimited revision history — never capped on any tier.
tierAvailability.professional: Unlimited line items and revisions, plus full approval routing on the RFQ.
tierAvailability.enterprise: Unlimited line items and revisions, plus custom workflow routing.

faqs.q: What is the current status?
faqs.a: In development, at approximately 5 percent, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 2. Today you can quote from an enquiry, but the enquiry is not yet a record of its own.

faqs.q: Can I quote from an enquiry today?
faqs.a: Yes. The quote editor is live and you can raise a quote from an emailed or captured enquiry now. What is missing is the RFQ record underneath it.

faqs.q: Will there be a limit on RFQ line items?
faqs.a: No. A 400-line RFQ will cost the same as a 4-line one on every tier, including Starter. That is a locked commitment in our pricing.

faqs.q: Why does no-quote matter?
faqs.a: Because a shop that declines a third of its enquiries has a targeting problem worth knowing about. Without an RFQ record, those declines are invisible.

faqs.q: Does this depend on anything else shipping first?
faqs.a: The multi-item RFQ header is being built alongside it, and technical pre-sales routing and the drawing revision work sit on top of it.

items.name: Multi-item RFQ header
items.metaDescription: A single RFQ header carrying many requested parts, each with its own quantity, drawing and date, so a 60-part enquiry is one record. Target Wave 1 M2.
items.lead: A buyer sending sixty part numbers in one email should produce one enquiry, not sixty. The header-and-lines structure for that is specified and scheduled, and not yet started.
items.answer: The multi-item RFQ header gives the KanchanFlow RFQ-to-Order CRM one enquiry record carrying many requested parts, each with its own quantity, drawing revision and required date. It is at 0 percent — specified and scheduled for Wave 1 Milestone 2, with no development work done yet. We would rather say that than imply it is underway.
summary: Large buyers do not send one part at a time. A tier-one supplier consolidating a programme will send a spreadsheet with sixty line items, mixed materials and staggered required dates, and expect one response. Handling that as sixty separate enquiries makes the response slow and the follow-up impossible to manage.

The header-and-lines structure treats the enquiry as one record with many part lines underneath it. Each line has its own quantity, drawing, revision and required date, and can be quoted, declined or deferred independently, while the header carries the buyer, the programme and the overall response deadline. The buyer gets one coherent answer rather than sixty separate replies.

capabilities.title: One header, many part lines
capabilities.body: The enquiry is a single record. Each requested part is a line with its own quantity, material, drawing reference and required date.

capabilities.title: Line-level disposition
capabilities.body: Quote forty lines, decline twelve on capacity and defer eight pending a drawing. The buyer gets one coherent response instead of silence on the parts you cannot do.

capabilities.title: Bulk import from a buyer spreadsheet
capabilities.body: Buyers send Excel. Importing their file into RFQ lines removes the retyping step where most of the errors and most of the delay come from.

capabilities.title: Quantity breaks per line
capabilities.body: Buyers frequently ask for pricing at several volumes on each part. Those breaks belong on the line, not as separate enquiries.

capabilities.title: Programme-level grouping
capabilities.body: The header can carry the customer's programme or project reference, so related enquiries over a year can be seen together.

capabilities.title: Staggered required dates per line
capabilities.body: Large buyers rarely want everything at once. Each line carries its own required date, so a schedule spread across nine months is captured on the enquiry rather than negotiated again after the quote goes out.

howItWorks.name: Create the RFQ header
howItWorks.text: Buyer, contact, programme reference, source and the overall required response date go on the header.

howItWorks.name: Import or enter the lines
howItWorks.text: Import the buyer's spreadsheet or enter parts manually. Each line carries part number, description, quantity, material and required date.

howItWorks.name: Attach drawings per line
howItWorks.text: Prints attach to the specific line they describe, with the revision letter recorded, so pricing is tied to a known revision.

howItWorks.name: Set line dispositions
howItWorks.text: Mark each line to quote, decline or defer. The header shows the split so nobody sends a partial answer by accident.

howItWorks.name: Raise the quote
howItWorks.text: Quotable lines carry into a quote in one action, keeping their quantities, drawings and dates.

tierAvailability.starter: Unlimited RFQ line items, never capped.
tierAvailability.professional: Unlimited line items, plus quantity breaks and alternate variants at quoting.
tierAvailability.enterprise: Unlimited line items, plus custom fields on the header and lines.

faqs.a: Raise a quote with sixty lines in the live quote editor. What you cannot do yet is hold the enquiry as one RFQ record with per-line dispositions.

faqs.a: No. Unlimited RFQ line items on every tier is a locked pricing commitment, including on Starter.

faqs.q: Will you import buyer spreadsheets?
faqs.a: That is in the specification, because retyping a buyer's Excel file is where the delay and the errors come from. It is not built yet.

faqs.q: How does this relate to RFQ management?
faqs.a: This is the header-and-lines structure; RFQ management is the record, the ownership and the outcome tracking. They are being built for the same milestone.

items.name: Technical pre-sales routing
items.h1: Technical pre-sales routing to engineering, costing and production
items.metaDescription: Route an RFQ that needs engineering, costing or production input to the right person with a deadline, and track what came back. Target Wave 1 M3.
items.lead: The enquiry that needs the toolroom's opinion before it can be priced. Route it, put a date on it, and see it come back — instead of chasing it in a corridor.
items.answer: Technical pre-sales routing sends a KanchanFlow RFQ to engineering, costing or production for input before it can be quoted, with a named owner and a deadline on each request. It is roughly 20 percent complete and targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 3, and it is the reason most complex quotes take three weeks instead of three days.
summary: The slowest quotes in a job shop are not the ones nobody worked on. They are the ones waiting on someone else — the toolmaker who has to say whether the fixture exists, the process engineer who has to confirm the tolerance is achievable, the buyer who has to price an unusual material. That waiting happens in corridors and unanswered emails.

The work in progress makes those requests explicit. An estimator routes the RFQ, or a line on it, to a named person with a question and a date. That person sees it on their home screen, answers it against the record, and the estimator sees the response land. The elapsed time on each request is measured, so bottlenecks stop being anecdotes.

capabilities.title: Route to a named person with a deadline
capabilities.body: Not a shared inbox or a shrug. The request goes to a person, with a question and a required-by date, and appears on their home screen until it is answered.

capabilities.title: Route a line, not just the whole enquiry
capabilities.body: On a multi-part RFQ only two lines may need engineering input. Routing at line level means the other fifty-eight can be quoted while those two are reviewed.

capabilities.title: Structured responses on the record
capabilities.body: The answer — feasible, feasible with a change, not feasible, plus estimated cost or tooling requirement — is written on the RFQ where the estimator will read it.

capabilities.title: Elapsed-time measurement
capabilities.body: Time spent waiting on engineering, costing and production is measured separately from time spent estimating, which is the only way to know where the three weeks went.

capabilities.title: Approval routing tie-in
capabilities.body: Where the technical answer changes the price beyond a threshold, the quote picks up the approval rules rather than going out on the estimator's judgement alone.

howItWorks.name: Estimator flags what they cannot answer
howItWorks.text: While working an RFQ, the estimator marks the lines or questions needing engineering, costing or production input.

howItWorks.name: Route with a question and a date
howItWorks.text: Each request goes to a named reviewer with a specific question and a required-by date, rather than a forwarded email saying 'thoughts?'.

howItWorks.name: Reviewer answers on the record
howItWorks.text: The request appears on the reviewer's home screen. They answer with a structured verdict and any cost or tooling implication.

howItWorks.name: Estimator prices with the answer
howItWorks.text: The response is attached to the RFQ line, so the quote is priced against a recorded technical position rather than a remembered conversation.

howItWorks.name: Measure the wait
howItWorks.text: Turnaround per reviewer and per request type is reported, so the shop can see which review step is the actual constraint.

tierAvailability.starter: Not included — Starter has no approval or routing engine.
tierAvailability.professional: Included with the full rules-based approval engine.
tierAvailability.enterprise: Included with full rules plus custom workflow routing.

faqs.a: About 20 percent, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 3. The routing model is built; the reviewer experience and the elapsed-time reporting are not finished.

faqs.a: That is the design, and it matters on multi-part enquiries where only two lines are unusual. It is not usable yet.

faqs.q: Which tiers will have it?
faqs.a: Professional and Enterprise. It depends on the approval engine, which Starter does not include.

faqs.q: Does the reviewer need a full seat?
faqs.a: Yes, a reviewer is a user with a role. We do not currently have a cheaper limited-participation seat, and we will not pretend one exists.

faqs.q: What does it measure?
faqs.a: Time waiting on each reviewer and each request type, separately from estimating time. That split is what tells you whether the delay is your desk or the toolroom.

items.name: Drawing revision management
items.h1: Drawing revision management with AI spec extraction
items.metaTitle: Drawing revision management, AI spec extraction
items.metaDescription: Track which drawing revision each quote and order was priced against, and extract key specs from the print with AI review. In development, target Wave 1 M3.
items.lead: Rev C came in after you quoted Rev B, and nobody noticed until the parts were on the inspection table. This is the record that stops that happening.
items.answer: Drawing revision management tracks which print revision every KanchanFlow quote, order and dispatch was priced and made against, and uses AI to extract key specifications from the drawing for a human to confirm. It is roughly 40 percent complete, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 3, and depends on your AI credit allowance.
summary: Revision drift is the most expensive silent failure in contract manufacturing. The customer issues Rev C, someone files it, the job runs to Rev B, and the cost surfaces at first-article inspection or, worse, at the customer's line. It is almost never anybody's fault in particular, which is exactly why a record beats a process.

The work in progress stores drawings as revisions rather than as files, stamps each quote and order with the revision it was priced against, and flags when a newer revision arrives on a part with open work. Alongside it, AI extraction reads material, finish, tolerance callouts and quantity from the print and presents them for confirmation next to the source.

capabilities.title: Revisions, not files
capabilities.body: A part has a drawing with revisions A, B, C. Uploading Rev C does not overwrite Rev B — both remain, and every document stamped with a revision keeps pointing at the right one.

capabilities.title: Quotes and orders stamped with a revision
capabilities.body: Every quote line and order line records the drawing revision it was priced or released against, which is the fact that settles a dispute in one screen.

capabilities.title: New revision alerts on open work
capabilities.body: When a newer revision lands on a part with an open quote or a running order, the affected records are flagged rather than quietly becoming wrong.

capabilities.title: AI extraction of key specifications
capabilities.body: Material, finish, general tolerance, critical callouts and quantity are extracted from the print and shown next to the region they came from for a person to confirm.

capabilities.title: Revision history on the part
capabilities.body: The full revision history sits on the part record, so you can see what changed and when across the life of a programme.

howItWorks.name: Upload the print against a part
howItWorks.text: The drawing is attached to the part with its revision letter and date, rather than being dropped into a quote as a loose file.

howItWorks.name: AI extracts the specifications
howItWorks.text: Material, finish, tolerances and quantity are read from the drawing. Extraction consumes AI credits at the published spec-sheet OCR weight of three credits per page.

howItWorks.name: A person confirms
howItWorks.text: Each extracted value is shown against the region of the drawing it came from. You confirm or correct it. Nothing is priced from an unconfirmed extraction.

howItWorks.name: Quote against the revision
howItWorks.text: The quote line records which revision it was priced against, and that stamp carries into the order created from it.

howItWorks.name: Handle the next revision
howItWorks.text: When Rev C arrives, it is added as a new revision and every open quote or order on that part is flagged for review.

tierAvailability.starter: Not included — Starter has no vector search or extraction beyond the two basic agents.
tierAvailability.professional: Included, with extraction running against your 500 credits per user per month.
tierAvailability.enterprise: Included, with extraction against your committed credit pool and custom prompts. A PLM connector for SolidWorks or Autodesk is available as an Enterprise add-on at $250 per month.

faqs.q: How complete is this?
faqs.a: About 40 percent, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 3. Revision storage and stamping are further along than the AI extraction, which is still being tuned.

faqs.q: Will the AI price the part?
faqs.a: No. It extracts specifications for a person to confirm. Pricing decisions stay with your estimator, and an unconfirmed extraction is never used.

faqs.q: What does extraction cost?
faqs.a: Three AI credits per page at the published spec-sheet OCR weight. Professional includes 500 credits per user per month; Enterprise runs on a committed pool.

faqs.q: What happens when a customer issues a new revision?
faqs.a: It is added as a new revision, and open quotes and orders stamped with the previous one are flagged for review. That flag is the whole point of the feature.

faqs.q: Is this a PLM system?
faqs.a: No. There is no engineering change order workflow, no approval routing on the drawing itself, and no CAD integration. It records which revision commercial documents were built on.

items.name: Manufacturing CPQ
items.h1: Manufacturing CPQ Lite — cost buildup, quantity breaks and margin floors
items.metaDescription: CPQ Lite for job shops: 4-column cost buildup, quantity breaks, alternates, a margin floor and discount approvals. In development, target Wave 1 M4.
items.lead: Where the price comes from, written down. Material, labour, outside process and overhead in four columns, quantity breaks off the same structure, and a floor that stops the Friday-afternoon line going out at four points of margin.
items.answer: Manufacturing CPQ is the estimating layer of the KanchanFlow RFQ-to-Order CRM: a four-column cost buildup — material, labour, outside process, overhead — with quantity breaks, alternates and a margin floor. It is CPQ Lite for job shops, not an enterprise configure-price-quote suite. Roughly 30 percent built, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 4.
summary: Two things are true about quoting in KanchanFlow today, and it matters which is which. The quote itself is live and in production: line items, drawings and material certificates attached to the record, a share link the buyer opens without a login, multi-currency with the FX rate locked onto the quote at the moment you price it, US sales tax and India GST rates, e-signed acceptance, and unlimited revision history on every tier including Starter. What is still in development is the estimating engine underneath it — the four-column cost buildup, quantity-break tiers, alternate variants, structured BOM roll-up, the margin floor and the rules-based approval engine. That work is roughly 30 percent complete and targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 4.

We call it CPQ Lite deliberately, and the distinction is not marketing. KanchanFlow is not an ERP, MRP, CAD, BOM or advanced CPQ system. We are not building a rival to Salesforce CPQ, PROS or Conga, and we will not pretend otherwise on a feature page. Those suites exist to configure a catalogue product across thousands of valid option permutations and to price a licence or a subscription against a rate card. A job shop has a different problem: one print, one material, six operations, an outside plater, and a number that has to hold for sixty days while steel moves. CPQ Lite is the five things an estimator pricing a machined part actually needs — cost buildup, quantity breaks, alternates, margin guardrails and revisions — and deliberately nothing beyond them.

The buildup has four columns because a shop carries four kinds of cost. Material is weight times rate plus scrap allowance, taken from the stock form you are actually buying rather than the finished part weight. Labour is setup plus cycle time per operation at your own machine and labour rates, with setup amortised across the quantity — which is exactly why the 500-piece unit price is lower than the 100-piece one, and why a quantity break is a calculation rather than a concession. Outside process is the plating, heat treat, anodise, passivation or NDT you buy in, held as its own column so a vendor increase is visible instead of being smeared into overhead. Overhead applies on the basis you choose. Margin sits on top of the four, against a floor.

Pricing is a hierarchy, not a single lookup, and the order is fixed: contract price first, then customer price, then the quantity break, then the standard cost buildup. If the part sits on a negotiated contract price list that is in effect on the quote date, that price wins and the buildup does not get a vote. If there is no contract but the customer carries their own agreed price for the part, that comes next. If neither exists, the quantity-break ladder for the part applies at the quantity being quoted. The cost buildup is the fallback — the answer when nothing has been agreed yet — not the first answer. Estimators get this wrong in spreadsheets constantly, quoting a standard price to an account that negotiated a lower one eighteen months ago and then honouring the mistake.

Discount authority is a threshold by role rather than a habit. A salesperson can discount to a set percentage; an inside sales manager further; a sales director further again; below the margin floor is the owner or the general manager and nobody else. A quote that goes past the holder's threshold cannot be finalised or sent until the named approver has approved it, and the approval is recorded on the quote with the approver, the timestamp, the depth of the discount and the reason given. There is no silent override. Where an emergency override exists it is available to authorised users and it is logged as an override, because an undocumented back door defeats the point of having thresholds at all.

Every quote carries a revision number, Rev 0 through Rev n, and historical pricing is never overwritten. When you re-quote at a new material rate, the old revision keeps the rate, the buildup, the margin, the approvals and the exact document that was sent. This is not a storage nicety. Eighteen months after a job, when a buyer holds a purchase order against Rev 3 and your material has moved twenty percent, you have to be able to answer one question without argument: why did this quote carry this price on the day it was sent. Revision history is what answers it, which is why we never cap it or expire it on any tier — Starter, Professional and Enterprise all keep the full chain, and the pricing page carries that as a guarantee rather than an upgrade lever.

capabilities.title: Live today: the quote the buildup feeds
capabilities.body: Line items with part number, quantity, unit price and lead time, drawings and certificates attached to the record, a browser share link the buyer opens without a login, open timestamps, and a validity window that expires the quote rather than letting somebody book an order against March material pricing.

capabilities.title: Live today: multi-currency with the rate locked on
capabilities.body: Quote a Canadian or Mexican customer in their currency and the FX rate is captured on the quote when you price it. It does not drift between quote and order. Re-rating is an explicit act on a new revision, so the customer sees what changed and why.

capabilities.title: Live today: unlimited revision history on every tier
capabilities.body: Rev 0 through Rev n, never trimmed, never expired, on Starter as well as Enterprise. Each revision keeps its own pricing, its own approvals and the exact document that went out. This is the mechanism behind the historical-pricing guarantee on the pricing page.

capabilities.title: Live today: tax rates and e-signed acceptance
capabilities.body: US sales tax rates and the full India GST, HSN and e-Invoice suite apply on the quote and the invoice that follows it. Acceptance through the share link records the accepting contact, timestamp and IP, and where a legally valid signature is required the quote routes through Aadhaar eSign and the signed revision locks.

capabilities.title: Building: the four-column cost buildup
capabilities.body: Material, labour, outside process and overhead as four separate visible columns, with margin on top. When a buyer pushes back on price you can see which column has room in it, and when a vendor raises plating you can see which quotes it touches.

capabilities.title: Building: quantity-break pricing tiers
capabilities.body: Quote 100, 500 and 1,000 from one buildup. Setup amortises across each break, so the ladder falls for a reason you can show the buyer rather than because somebody rounded down. The customer sees three prices; you maintain one calculation.

capabilities.title: Building: alternate variants on the same enquiry
capabilities.body: Price the 6061-T6 version and the 304 stainless version, or the machined-from-bar and the near-net-casting route, as alternates on the same quote. The buyer picks; you do not maintain three quote documents that drift apart by Wednesday.

capabilities.title: Building: structured BOM with parent-child roll-up
capabilities.body: A weldment made of six machined details and two purchased parts prices as a parent with children. Each child carries its own buildup and the parent rolls up, so an assembly price is traceable to the details rather than being one typed number.

capabilities.title: Building: margin guardrails with a floor
capabilities.body: A minimum margin per product family, per customer or globally. A line that prices below the floor flags in the editor while the estimator can still act on it, and either warns or blocks depending on the rule. Every below-floor line that went out is reportable, with who approved it.

capabilities.title: Building: the rules an estimator actually needs
capabilities.body: Option compatibility, dependency, exclusion, visibility and mandatory-field validation — five rule types, not a constraint solver. They exist to stop an unmakeable or incomplete quote leaving the building, not to generate configurations.

capabilities.title: Building: the pricing hierarchy, applied in order
capabilities.body: Contract price, then customer price, then quantity break, then the standard cost buildup. The line shows which level it priced from, so an estimator can see at a glance that this part came off a contract list expiring in March rather than off the buildup.

capabilities.title: Building: discount approval thresholds by role
capabilities.body: Each role carries a discount ceiling. Past it, the quote cannot be finalised until the named approver approves, and the decision is written onto the quote with the approver, timestamp, discount depth and reason. Approvals are actionable from the mobile app so a job does not wait for someone to reach a laptop.

howItWorks.name: Configure
howItWorks.text: The estimator opens the RFQ line and configures the part as it was actually asked for: material and temper, stock form, the operation list, finish, tolerance class, heat treat, marking, packaging, and the quantity or quantities the buyer wants priced. A repeat part starts from the last accepted revision rather than a blank line, so a reorder is a check rather than a re-estimate.

howItWorks.name: Validate
howItWorks.text: The rules run before anything is priced. Compatibility blocks a combination that cannot be made — black anodise is not available on 304 stainless, so it is not offered on a 304 part. Dependency pulls in what a choice requires: a bore held to ±0.0005 in adds a CMM inspection operation to the buildup instead of being remembered on the shop floor three weeks later. Exclusion removes what a choice rules out. Visibility hides options that do not apply to the material selected. Mandatory-field validation holds the quote until the drawing revision, quantity and required date are present, so an incomplete quote cannot be sent.

howItWorks.name: Price
howItWorks.text: Pricing walks the hierarchy in order. Contract price first: if this customer has a negotiated price list in effect on the quote date, that is the price. Then customer price, then the quantity-break ladder at the quantity being quoted. Only if none of those apply does the four-column buildup run — material from weight and rate plus scrap, labour from setup and cycle at your machine rates with setup amortised over the quantity, outside process from your vendor cost, overhead on your chosen basis, margin on top. The buildup is the fallback, not the first answer.

howItWorks.name: Review
howItWorks.text: The margin floor is checked line by line. A line below the floor flags before the quote can be sent, and a discount past the estimator's role threshold routes to the named approver with the buildup, the floor and the shortfall visible. Until that approval lands the quote cannot be finalised. The decision — approver, timestamp, depth, reason — is written onto the quote and, on Enterprise, into the immutable audit log.

howItWorks.name: Quote
howItWorks.text: The approved buildup becomes a quote document the buyer recognises: line items, quantity breaks side by side, alternates where you offered them, lead times, tooling, validity window, tax and terms. Your team sees the cost structure; the customer copy shows the price. One record, two views — the buildup never appears on the document that leaves the building.

howItWorks.name: Send
howItWorks.text: Send it as a share link by email or WhatsApp rather than a 6 MB attachment that a mail filter eats. The buyer opens it in a browser, you get the open timestamp and view count, and the follow-up cadence starts the moment it leaves. Acceptance happens on the link, and the accepted revision locks.

howItWorks.name: Track
howItWorks.text: The open quote book ages, follow-ups run on the cadence you set, and every change makes a new revision with the previous one preserved intact. Win or lose, the quote keeps the price, the buildup, the rate, the approvals and the document as they were on the day it was sent. That is what lets you answer the buyer eighteen months later without opening a mail archive.

tierAvailability.starter: 2-column basic cost buildup. No quantity breaks, no structured BOM, no alternate variants and no approval engine. Unlimited revision history and unlimited RFQ line items are included, as on every tier.
tierAvailability.professional: 4-column cost buildup with margin guardrails, plus quantity breaks, structured BOM, alternate variants and the full-rules approval engine.
tierAvailability.enterprise: 4-column cost buildup with custom columns and custom cost bases, plus quantity breaks, structured BOM, alternate variants, and the approval engine with custom workflows.

faqs.q: What can I actually use today, and what is still being built?
faqs.a: Live today: the quote editor, line items, attachments, share links, multi-currency with a locked FX rate, unlimited revision history, US sales tax and India GST rates, and e-signed acceptance. In development: the four-column cost buildup, quantity breaks, alternate variants, structured BOM roll-up, margin guardrails and the approval engine. That second list is about 30 percent complete against Wave 1 Milestone 4.

faqs.q: Is this CPQ in the enterprise software sense?
faqs.a: No. Our anti-position says plainly that KanchanFlow is not an ERP, MRP, CAD, BOM or advanced CPQ system, and that still holds. This is CPQ Lite: cost buildup, quantity breaks, alternates, margin guardrails and revisions for a shop pricing a machined part. If you need a catalogue configurator with a constraint solver and licence rate cards, buy Salesforce CPQ, PROS or Conga — we are not a substitute for them and will not sell ourselves as one.

faqs.q: Which price wins when a customer has a contract price?
faqs.a: The contract price, if a negotiated list is in effect on the quote date. The order is fixed: contract price, then customer price, then the quantity break, then the standard cost buildup. The buildup is the fallback when nothing has been agreed, not the first answer, and the line shows which level it priced from.

faqs.q: What happens if a discount goes past my threshold?
faqs.a: The quote cannot be finalised or sent until the named approver for that threshold approves it. The approval is recorded on the quote with the approver, timestamp, discount depth and reason, and on Enterprise it also lands in the immutable audit log. An emergency override is available to authorised users and is logged as an override rather than as a normal approval.

faqs.q: Do you overwrite old prices when a rate changes?
faqs.a: Never. A new material rate applies to new revisions. Rev 0 keeps the rate, buildup, margin, approvals and exact document it went out with, and so does every revision after it. The point is to be able to answer why a quote carried the price it did on the day it was sent, and that answer has to survive the rate change that came after.

faqs.q: Does setup really amortise across the quantity?
faqs.a: Yes, and that is the whole reason a quantity break is a calculation rather than a discount. Setup is spread across the break quantity in the labour column, so the ladder from 100 to 500 to 1,000 falls for a reason you can put in front of a buyer.

faqs.q: Which tiers get the four-column buildup?
faqs.a: Professional and Enterprise. Starter keeps a two-column basic buildup with no quantity breaks, no structured BOM and no alternate variants. Enterprise adds custom columns and custom cost bases. Unlimited revision history and unlimited RFQ line items are on every tier, including Starter, and always will be.

items.name: Contract and customer price lists
items.h1: Contract and customer price lists with effective dates
items.metaDescription: Negotiated price lists locked to a customer or dealer, with effective and expiry dates, that take precedence over the standard cost buildup. Target Wave 1 M4.
items.lead: The price you agreed in March, honoured in November without anybody having to remember it. A list against the customer, dated, that the quote reads before it reads your cost buildup.
items.answer: Contract price lists in the KanchanFlow RFQ-to-Order CRM hold negotiated prices against a customer or dealer, with effective and expiry dates, and take precedence over the standard cost buildup when a quote is priced. It is the first level of the CPQ pricing hierarchy, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 4 alongside the buildup itself.
summary: Every shop with repeat customers has agreed prices, and almost nobody has them anywhere the estimator can see at the moment of quoting. They live in a signed supply agreement in a filing cabinet, an email thread from two purchasing managers ago, or one person's memory. The failure is predictable in both directions: you quote a standard price to an account that negotiated ten percent off and then honour the mistake, or you quote the agreed price for a part on an agreement that expired in June and lose the increase you were entitled to take.

A contract price list fixes that by putting the agreement in the system, against the customer or dealer it belongs to, with the dates it is valid between. When an estimator prices a part for that account, the quote reads the list before it reads anything else. The line shows that it priced from a contract list rather than from the buildup, and it shows which list and when that list expires — so an estimator quoting in February can see that the agreement runs out in March and raise it before the buyer does.

The order of precedence is the same one the manufacturing CPQ work uses, and it is fixed: contract price, then customer price, then quantity break, then the standard cost buildup. A contract list is the strongest of the four because it is the one you signed. The buildup is the fallback for parts nobody has agreed a price for yet. This is why the two pieces of work carry the same milestone — a pricing hierarchy with a missing top level is not a hierarchy.

The uncomfortable case is a contract price below your margin floor, and it happens: material moved, or the agreement was signed at a volume that never materialised. We do not silently suppress the floor because a contract exists, and we do not block a quote you are contractually obliged to honour. The line prices at the contract price, flags as below floor with the shortfall shown against the current buildup, and routes for approval by the same rule as any other below-floor line. The exception is recorded. What that gives you is a list, at renewal time, of every contract line you are currently losing money on — which is the conversation the agreement renewal should actually start from.

Dealers work the same way. A distributor buying at a channel discount carries their own list, dated, so a partner order priced through the portal and a partner order priced at your desk produce the same number. Where a dealer holds exclusivity on a SKU, the exclusivity rules and the price list are two separate records and stay that way: one says who may sell it, the other says at what price.

capabilities.title: A list locked to a customer or a dealer
capabilities.body: Prices attach to the account, not to the part in general. Two customers can carry different agreed prices for the same part number and neither can see the other. A dealer list and a direct-customer list are the same object with a different owner.

capabilities.title: Effective and expiry dates on every line
capabilities.body: A price is valid between two dates. Quotes dated inside the window use it, quotes outside it fall through to the next level of the hierarchy, and an estimator quoting near the end sees the expiry on the line rather than finding out afterwards.

capabilities.title: Precedence over the standard cost buildup
capabilities.body: Contract price, then customer price, then quantity break, then buildup. A part on an in-force contract list prices from the list, and the line records which list it came from so the number is traceable at renewal or in a dispute.

capabilities.title: Below-floor contract prices flagged, not hidden
capabilities.body: When an agreed price sits under your current margin floor, the line prices at the agreed number, flags with the shortfall against today's buildup, and routes for approval like any other below-floor line. You honour the contract and you can see what it is costing.

capabilities.title: Quantity breaks inside a contract list
capabilities.body: An agreement that says one price to 500 pieces and another above it holds both. The break ladder sits inside the list rather than being a separate arrangement somebody has to remember to apply.

capabilities.title: Renewal exposure in one report
capabilities.body: Which agreements expire in the next ninety days, which lines are below floor, and how much revenue is priced off each list. That report is the agenda for the renewal meeting rather than a task somebody does the week the agreement lapses.

capabilities.title: Currency and unit held on the list
capabilities.body: A list carries its own currency and unit of measure so a USD agreement with a Mexican customer does not get re-rated by a quote in pesos. FX on the quote is locked at pricing time, as it is on every quote today.

howItWorks.name: Load the agreement
howItWorks.text: Create a list against the customer or dealer and enter the agreed part numbers and prices, or import them from the spreadsheet the agreement was negotiated in. Each line carries its price, its unit, its currency and any quantity breaks the agreement includes.

howItWorks.name: Set the window
howItWorks.text: Give the list an effective date and an expiry date. A list with no expiry is a decision you make explicitly rather than a default, because an agreement nobody ever reviews is how a shop ends up quoting 2024 prices in 2027.

howItWorks.name: Quote against it
howItWorks.text: When an estimator prices a part for that account inside the window, the quote reads the contract list first. The line shows the price, the list it came from and the expiry date, so nothing about the number is a mystery.

howItWorks.name: Handle the exceptions
howItWorks.text: If the contract price is below your current margin floor, the line flags with the shortfall against the buildup and routes for approval by the standard rule. If the part is not on the list, pricing falls through to customer price, then quantity break, then the four-column buildup.

howItWorks.name: Watch the expiry
howItWorks.text: Lists approaching expiry surface before they lapse, with the revenue priced off them and the lines currently under floor. Renewal starts from evidence rather than from whichever price the buyer remembers.

howItWorks.name: Keep the history
howItWorks.text: A superseded list is kept, not overwritten. A quote sent in April against the old agreement still shows the old price and the list it came from, which is how you answer a question about that quote two years later.

tierAvailability.starter: Not available. Starter prices from the 2-column basic cost buildup and has no quantity breaks.
tierAvailability.professional: Included, with dated contract and customer lists, quantity breaks inside a list, and below-floor flagging through the margin guardrails.
tierAvailability.enterprise: Included, with custom cost bases and multi-entity price lists across plants.

faqs.q: What is the order of precedence?
faqs.a: Contract price, then customer price, then quantity break, then the standard cost buildup. A contract list is the strongest because it is the one you signed. The buildup is the fallback for parts where nothing has been agreed.

faqs.q: What happens when a contract price is below my margin floor?
faqs.a: The line prices at the contract price — you agreed it — and flags as below floor with the shortfall shown against today's buildup. It routes for approval like any other below-floor line and the exception is recorded, so at renewal you have a list of exactly which lines are losing money.

faqs.q: What happens when a list expires mid-quote?
faqs.a: Pricing uses the quote date. A quote dated inside the window prices from the list; a quote dated after it falls through to the next level of the hierarchy. Lists nearing expiry surface in advance so the renewal conversation happens before the lapse, not after.

faqs.q: Can dealers have their own lists?
faqs.a: Yes. A distributor list is the same object owned by a channel partner, so a partner order priced in the portal and one priced at your desk give the same number. Exclusivity on a SKU is a separate record from the price of it.

faqs.q: Do you keep old lists?
faqs.a: Yes. A superseded list is retained rather than overwritten, and a quote sent against it still shows the price and the list it came from. Historical pricing is never rewritten on this site, in any feature.

faqs.q: Which tiers get this?
faqs.a: Professional and Enterprise, alongside the four-column buildup and quantity breaks it extends. Starter prices from the two-column basic buildup.

faqs.q: Is any of this available today?
faqs.a: No. It is in development against Wave 1 Milestone 4, the same milestone as the manufacturing CPQ work, and that date is inherited from it rather than separately committed. What is live today is the quote editor around it: line items, attachments, share links, locked FX and unlimited revisions.

items.name: Margin guardrails
items.metaDescription: Set a margin floor per product family or customer and have quote lines flag or block below it, with approval routing on the exception. Target Wave 1 M4.
items.lead: The line that went out at four percent because it was Friday. A floor per family or customer, a flag when a line crosses it, and an approval on the exception.
items.answer: Margin guardrails put a minimum margin on KanchanFlow quote lines, by product family or customer, and flag or route for approval any line that falls below the floor. It is at 0 percent — specified and scheduled for Wave 1 Milestone 4, with no development work started. It will be a Professional and Enterprise capability.
summary: Margin leaks a line at a time. Nobody approves a bad quarter; they approve twelve individually defensible concessions, each made late in the day by somebody who wanted the job. By the time it shows up in the numbers, the quotes are out and the orders are booked. By then the only remaining option is to price the next job better.

The specified behaviour is simple and deliberately not clever. You set a margin floor by product family, by customer, or globally. When a quote line prices below it, the line flags in the editor before the quote is sent, and depending on your rules it either warns or requires an approval from a named person. The exception is recorded either way.

capabilities.title: Floors by family, customer or globally
capabilities.body: A machined component family may carry a different floor from a fabricated assembly, and a strategic account may carry a lower one deliberately. The rule should match the reality.

capabilities.title: Flag at the line, before the send
capabilities.body: The warning appears on the line in the editor while the estimator can still do something about it, not in a report at month end.

capabilities.title: Warn or block, your choice
capabilities.body: Some shops want a warning and a record. Others want the quote to stop until someone senior approves. Both are configurable per rule.

capabilities.title: Approval routing on the exception
capabilities.body: Below-floor lines route to a named approver with the buildup, the floor and the shortfall shown, using the same approval engine as discount approvals.

capabilities.title: Exception reporting
capabilities.body: Every below-floor line that was sent, who approved it and why, in one list. That report is the conversation you cannot have today.

howItWorks.name: Define the floors
howItWorks.text: Set a default margin floor and any overrides by product family or customer. Rules are held centrally rather than in individual heads.

howItWorks.name: Estimator prices the line
howItWorks.text: As the four-column buildup produces a margin, the line is compared against the applicable floor in real time.

howItWorks.name: The line flags
howItWorks.text: A line below the floor is marked with the floor, the actual margin and the shortfall. Nothing is hidden and nothing is silently corrected.

howItWorks.name: Approve or reprice
howItWorks.text: Depending on the rule, the estimator reprices or routes the line for approval. The approver sees the buildup and the shortfall, not just a discount percentage.

howItWorks.name: Review the exceptions
howItWorks.text: Approved exceptions report by customer, product family and approver, so a pattern of concessions is visible while it is still fixable.

tierAvailability.professional: Included as part of the 4-column buildup with the full rules-based approval engine.
tierAvailability.enterprise: Included, with custom thresholds and custom approval workflows.

faqs.q: Is any of this built?
faqs.a: No. It is at 0 percent, specified and scheduled for Wave 1 Milestone 4. It depends on the four-column buildup and the approval engine, both of which are further along.

faqs.q: Will it block a quote or just warn?
faqs.a: Both are configurable per rule. Some shops want a hard stop below the floor; others want a warning and a recorded exception.

faqs.q: Can different customers have different floors?
faqs.a: Yes, that is in the specification. A deliberately thin margin on a strategic account is a decision, not an accident, and the rules should reflect it.

faqs.q: Which tiers will have it?
faqs.a: Professional and Enterprise. It sits on the four-column buildup and the approval engine, neither of which is on Starter.

faqs.q: Does it recommend prices?
faqs.a: No. It enforces the floors you set. Recommending a price would require knowing your customer's alternatives, and we do not.

items.name: Quote revision diff
items.metaDescription: Compare two quote revisions side by side and see exactly which lines, prices, quantities and lead times changed. In development, target Wave 1 M3.
items.lead: Rev 2 against Rev 4, line by line, with the changed values highlighted. The conversation that currently happens by opening two PDFs on two screens.
items.answer: Quote revision diff shows two KanchanFlow quote revisions side by side and highlights every changed line, price, quantity, lead time and term. It is roughly 20 percent complete, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 3. Basic visual comparison is planned for Starter, with full diff and change alerts on Professional and Enterprise.
summary: Quotes in manufacturing do not go out once. They go to Rev 5 as the customer changes quantities, the material moves, and the required date slips. By Rev 5 nobody can remember whether the tooling charge was in Rev 3, and the buyer certainly cannot. The argument that follows is expensive and entirely avoidable with a record.

The diff view answers that in one screen. Pick two revisions, see the lines that were added, removed or changed, and see the specific fields that moved. On Professional, change alerts flag material movements on price, quantity and lead time so a revision that quietly dropped a line does not go out unnoticed.

capabilities.title: Side-by-side revision comparison
capabilities.body: Any two revisions of the same quote, aligned line by line. Added, removed and changed lines are marked distinctly rather than left for you to spot.

capabilities.title: Field-level change highlighting
capabilities.body: Price, quantity, lead time, description and terms are compared individually, so a change of ten cents on line seven does not hide behind a matching total.

capabilities.title: Change alerts on material movements
capabilities.body: On Professional, changes above a threshold you set raise an alert before send, which catches the revision that dropped a line by accident.

capabilities.title: Diff summary for the customer conversation
capabilities.body: A short 'what changed since Rev 3' summary you can put in the covering message, so the buyer is not left to find it themselves.

capabilities.title: Full history, never trimmed
capabilities.body: Every revision remains comparable for the life of the record. We do not cap revision retention on any tier, including Starter.

howItWorks.name: Open the quote's revision list
howItWorks.text: Every revision of the quote is listed with its date, who created it and whether it was sent.

howItWorks.name: Pick two revisions
howItWorks.text: Choose the pair to compare — usually the last one the customer acknowledged against the one about to go out.

howItWorks.name: Read the diff
howItWorks.text: Lines align side by side with added, removed and changed lines marked, and the specific changed fields highlighted within each line.

howItWorks.name: Check the alerts
howItWorks.text: Material changes above your threshold are called out. On a long quote this is the difference between catching a dropped line and shipping the error.

howItWorks.name: Send with a change summary
howItWorks.text: Paste the change summary into the covering note so the buyer's engineer and buyer both know what moved.

tierAvailability.professional: Full diff with change alerts on price, quantity and lead time.
tierAvailability.enterprise: Full diff plus custom fields included in the comparison.

faqs.q: What can I do today?
faqs.a: Every revision is stored and viewable now, and Starter's basic visual comparison is the current level. The full side-by-side diff is about 20 percent built, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 3.

faqs.q: Is revision history limited on any tier?
faqs.a: No. Unlimited revision retention on every tier is a locked pricing commitment. The record of what you agreed to should never expire because of a plan.

faqs.q: Will it catch a line I deleted by mistake?
faqs.a: That is the main thing it is for. Removed lines are marked distinctly, and on Professional a removal above your threshold raises an alert before the quote sends.

faqs.q: Can the customer see the diff?
faqs.a: Not directly. You get a change summary you can include in the covering message, which is usually the more useful form for a buyer.

faqs.q: Does it compare attachments?
faqs.a: It compares the structured quote data. Drawing revision changes are tracked separately in drawing revision management, which is the right place for them.

items.name: Approval engine
items.metaDescription: Route discounts, below-floor margins, unusual terms and large orders to named approvers by rule, with the decision recorded. In development, target Wave 1 M4.
items.lead: Who has to say yes, when, and on what basis — written as rules rather than as a habit that breaks the week the owner is travelling.
items.answer: The approval engine routes KanchanFlow quotes, orders and exceptions to named approvers based on rules you define — discount depth, margin floor, order value, payment terms. It is roughly 40 percent complete, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 4, and it is the mechanism the margin guardrails and technical pre-sales routing both depend on.
summary: In most shops approval is a person. The owner sees the big quotes, usually, when they are not travelling, and everything else goes out on judgement. That works at fifteen quotes a week and fails at eighty, and the failure is invisible until you look at what actually shipped. By that point the discount has been given and the order is on the floor.

Rules make the same judgement repeatable. Discount above a percentage goes to the sales manager. Margin below the floor goes to the owner. Payment terms beyond thirty days go to finance. Order value above a threshold goes to two people in sequence. Each decision is recorded with who made it and when, on the record itself.

capabilities.title: Rules on the conditions that matter
capabilities.body: Discount percentage, margin against floor, order value, payment terms, lead-time commitment and customer credit status can each trigger a rule, alone or in combination.

capabilities.title: Sequential and parallel approvers
capabilities.body: Some approvals need two people in order; others need any one of a group. Both patterns are supported rather than forcing every rule into a single chain.

capabilities.title: Approve from the phone
capabilities.body: Pending approvals appear in the mobile app with the numbers that matter — price, cost, margin, customer history — so a decision does not wait for someone to reach a laptop.

capabilities.title: Decisions recorded on the record
capabilities.body: Approver, timestamp, decision and any comment are stored against the quote or order permanently, and on Enterprise into the immutable audit log.

capabilities.title: Escalation on delay
capabilities.body: An approval sitting untouched past its threshold escalates rather than quietly holding up a quote. The default failure mode of an approval workflow is silence, and escalation is what answers it.

capabilities.title: Override with a record, not a back door
capabilities.body: Where a genuine emergency needs an override, it is available to authorised users and it is recorded as an override. Undocumented back doors defeat the point of having rules.

howItWorks.name: Write the rules
howItWorks.text: Define conditions and the approver for each. Start with the two or three that matter — discount depth and margin floor are usually enough to begin with.

howItWorks.name: A quote hits a condition
howItWorks.text: As the estimator prices, the engine evaluates the rules. A quote that needs approval is marked before it can be sent, not after.

howItWorks.name: The approver is notified
howItWorks.text: The approval appears on the approver's home screen and in the mobile app with the full context — cost buildup, customer history, what is being asked.

howItWorks.name: The decision is recorded
howItWorks.text: Approve, reject or approve with a comment. The decision, the approver and the timestamp attach to the quote permanently.

howItWorks.name: The quote proceeds or returns
howItWorks.text: Approved quotes can send. Rejected ones return to the estimator with the reason attached rather than disappearing into a conversation.

tierAvailability.starter: Not included.
tierAvailability.professional: Full rules-based approval engine.
tierAvailability.enterprise: Full rules plus custom workflows, with decisions written to the immutable audit log.

faqs.q: How far along is it?
faqs.a: About 40 percent, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 4. Rule evaluation is built; the approver experience, escalation and mobile approvals are still in progress.

faqs.q: Can approvals be done on a phone?
faqs.a: That is the design, because the person who needs to approve is usually not at a desk. Mobile approval is part of the Milestone 4 scope.

faqs.q: What happens if an approver does nothing?
faqs.a: The approval escalates after a threshold you set. Silence is the normal failure mode of approval workflows, and it should not quietly cost you a job.

faqs.q: Is there an override?
faqs.a: Yes, for authorised users, and it is recorded as an override with a name and a timestamp. An undocumented back door would defeat the purpose of the rules.

faqs.q: Which tiers get it?
faqs.a: Professional and Enterprise. Starter does not include an approval engine, which is one of the clearer reasons a growing shop moves up a tier.

items.name: Customer 360
items.h1: Customer 360 with plants and stakeholder mapping
items.metaDescription: See a customer as a company with plants, buyers, engineers and quality contacts, plus quoting, order and payment history in one view. Target Wave 1 M4.
items.lead: One buyer at head office, two engineers at the plant in Ohio, a quality manager who can stop everything. A customer is a structure, and it should be recorded as one.
items.answer: Customer 360 models a KanchanFlow account as a company with plants, sites and mapped stakeholders rather than a single row, combining quoting, order, payment and conversation history in one view. It is roughly 60 percent complete, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 4, and it is the most advanced of the in-progress customer features.
summary: Manufacturing customers are not individuals. A tier-one supplier has a corporate purchasing office that negotiates, plants that release orders, engineers who decide whether your process is acceptable, and a quality manager who can stop shipments. Recording all of that as one company row loses every relationship that actually matters. It also loses the reason a deal was won, which is usually a person.

Customer 360 gives the account plants and sites, contacts with roles and influence, and a complete history of quotes, orders, payments and conversations across all of them. Starter keeps a basic single-level customer record; Professional adds plants and stakeholder mapping; Enterprise adds multi-entity roll-up for groups. The structure is built as work happens rather than maintained by hand in a spreadsheet.

capabilities.title: Plants and sites under one account
capabilities.body: A customer with four plants is one account with four sites, each with its own ship-to address, contacts and order history, rolled up to the parent.

capabilities.title: Stakeholder mapping with roles
capabilities.body: Buyer, engineer, quality, plant manager, accounts payable — each with their influence on the decision recorded. When your champion leaves, you can see who else you know.

capabilities.title: Complete commercial history
capabilities.body: Quotes raised, win rate, orders, dispatch performance, invoices, aging and outstanding balance in one view instead of five separate reports.

capabilities.title: Conversation history across channels
capabilities.body: Calls, WhatsApp threads, emails and visit records interleaved on one timeline, which is what a handover between salespeople actually requires.

capabilities.title: Part and programme history
capabilities.body: Which parts you have quoted and made for this customer, at what price, on which drawing revision. That history is what makes the repeat quote fast.

capabilities.title: Multi-entity roll-up on Enterprise
capabilities.body: Where the same customer group buys from several of your legal entities, Enterprise rolls exposure and history up across them.

howItWorks.name: Create the account
howItWorks.text: The parent company record holds the commercial relationship — terms, credit limit, currency and owner.

howItWorks.name: Add plants and sites
howItWorks.text: Each plant has its own address, contacts and delivery requirements, and its own order history under the parent.

howItWorks.name: Map the stakeholders

items.metaDescription: A full view of each dealer's ordering pattern, balance and health, with an AI agent predicting when a reorder is due. In development, target Wave 1 M5.
items.lead: A dealer who normally orders every six weeks has not ordered in eleven. Somebody should be calling them today, and this is the screen that says so.
items.answer: Dealer 360 brings each channel partner's ordering pattern, outstanding balance, portal activity and health into one view in the KanchanFlow RFQ-to-Order CRM, with an AI agent predicting when a reorder is due. It is roughly 50 percent complete, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 5, and it builds on the live channel partner records.
summary: Channel revenue does not usually fall off a cliff. A dealer quietly stretches from six weeks to nine to fourteen, and by the time the drop is visible in the quarter they have been buying from somebody else for three months. The signal was in the ordering pattern the whole time, and nobody was reading it.

Dealer 360 makes that pattern visible and adds an agent that predicts the expected reorder date from the partner's own history. When a dealer goes materially past their normal interval they surface for a call. The Dealer Health Agent scores each partner on ordering consistency, payment behaviour and engagement, with the components shown rather than hidden.

items.name: Dealer and territory exclusivity
items.h1: Dealer and territory exclusivity with channel-conflict rules
items.metaDescription: Assign a SKU exclusively to a dealer, lock a territory, and settle channel conflict when two dealers register the same customer. Target Wave 1 M5.
items.lead: Two dealers, one customer, one phone call to you. Exclusivity written down as a rule with a date on it, so the answer is the same whoever asks and whoever is in the room.
items.answer: Dealer and territory exclusivity in the KanchanFlow RFQ-to-Order CRM records which channel partner holds which SKUs and which territories, and applies channel-conflict rules when two dealers register the same customer. It extends the live dealer records and the territory tree, and is targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 5 alongside Dealer 360.
summary: Channel conflict is not an abstract governance problem. It is a Tuesday morning phone call from a distributor who has just found out that the account he has been developing for four months was quoted last week by another of your dealers at a lower number, and it usually ends with one of them going quiet on you. What makes it expensive is not the argument, it is that the answer depends on who you ask, and both dealers genuinely believe they are right because nothing was ever written down in a place both of them could see.

Exclusivity is the part that gets written down. A dealer holds named SKUs or product families, or holds a territory node, or both, between two dates. Where a right is exclusive, nobody else in the channel may be quoted for that combination — and the rule is visible to your inside sales desk at the moment they are about to break it, not in a distributor agreement in a drawer. Where the arrangement is non-exclusive, that is recorded too, because ambiguity is what produces the phone call.

Customer registration is the other half. A dealer registers a customer they are working; the registration carries a date, a scope and a lifespan. When a second dealer registers the same customer, the rule decides: first valid registration holds it for the protection period, the second dealer is told immediately rather than three months later, and if you want the case escalated to a human it goes to a named person with both registration dates, both pipelines and the territory position in front of them. The one thing it does not do is fail silently and let both partners keep spending money.

The structure this rides on is already there in shape. Channel partner records are live today. The five-level dealer hierarchy, the seven-level territory tree and the dealer portal are Professional and Enterprise capabilities, and Dealer 360 is in development against Wave 1 Milestone 5. Exclusivity is the rule layer on top of them, and it inherits that milestone rather than carrying a separately committed date of its own.

We are deliberate about what exclusivity does not become here. It is not a legal agreement, and nothing in the software creates or terminates a distributor contract. It is not price control either — what a dealer pays sits on a contract price list, and who is allowed to sell is a different question from what it costs. Keeping those two records separate is what stops an exclusivity change quietly repricing a channel.

capabilities.title: Exclusive SKU assignment
capabilities.body: A part number, a product family or a whole line assigned exclusively to one partner between two dates. Anyone quoting that SKU to another partner is stopped in the quote, with the holder and the expiry date named.

capabilities.title: Territory locks on the hierarchy
capabilities.body: Exclusivity attaches to a node in the seven-level territory tree, so a partner can hold a state, a city or a route without holding the region above it. Rights roll down the branch unless a child node is explicitly carved out.

capabilities.title: Channel-conflict rules with a stated resolution
capabilities.body: Overlap between two partners is either allowed, warned on, or blocked, and which one it is is a rule you set rather than a judgement made in the moment by whoever picked up the phone.

capabilities.title: Customer registration with a protection window
capabilities.body: A partner registers an account they are developing. The registration has a start date, a scope and a lifespan, and it expires rather than lasting forever on the strength of one visit in 2026.

capabilities.title: Duplicate registration handled at the moment it happens
capabilities.body: When a second partner registers the same customer, the first valid registration holds for its protection period and the second partner is told at once, with the reason. Contested cases escalate to a named person with both registration dates, both pipelines and the territory position visible.

capabilities.title: Direct-versus-channel visibility
capabilities.body: House accounts and direct-sale carve-outs are recorded on the same structure, so your own sales team is subject to the same rules as the channel and a partner can see which accounts are carved out before working one.

capabilities.title: Overrides with a record, not a back door
capabilities.body: Where you decide to quote against an exclusivity, an authorised user can override and the override is logged with who, when and why. On Enterprise it lands in the immutable audit log. Nobody has to reconstruct the decision later from memory.

howItWorks.name: Define what is exclusive
howItWorks.text: For each partner, record the SKUs or product families and the territory nodes they hold, whether each right is exclusive or non-exclusive, and the dates it runs between. Anything not recorded is open, and it says so rather than being assumed.

howItWorks.name: Set the conflict rule
howItWorks.text: Choose what happens on an overlap: allow it, warn the person quoting, or block the quote. Different product lines can carry different rules — a commodity line is often open while a configured machine is protected.

howItWorks.name: Partners register their customers
howItWorks.text: A partner registers an account through the portal with the opportunity they are working. The registration carries a scope, a start date and a protection period, so a claim on a customer has a shape and an end.

howItWorks.name: A second registration arrives
howItWorks.text: The rule runs immediately. The first valid registration holds for its window, the second partner receives the decision and the reason, and a contested case routes to your named channel manager with both partners' dates, pipelines and territory positions on one screen.

howItWorks.name: Quoting respects the position
howItWorks.text: When anyone — a partner or your own desk — starts a quote that crosses an exclusive right, the rule fires in the quote rather than in a report at month end. The holder, the expiry and the rule that fired are named on screen.

howItWorks.name: Rights expire and get reviewed
howItWorks.text: Exclusivity has an end date, and rights approaching expiry surface with the revenue and coverage behind them. A right that renews should renew on evidence of what the partner actually did with it.

faqs.q: What happens when two dealers register the same customer?
faqs.a: The first valid registration holds the account for its protection period and the second partner is told immediately, with the reason, rather than finding out after four months of work. If you have set the case to escalate, it goes to a named channel manager with both registration dates, both pipelines and the territory position on one screen.

faqs.q: Can a dealer hold a territory without holding everything under it?
faqs.a: Yes. Rights attach to a node in the seven-level tree and roll down the branch, but a child node can be carved out explicitly. A partner can hold a state while one city inside it stays a house account.

faqs.q: Does exclusivity block my own sales team?
faqs.a: It does if you set it to. House accounts and direct-sale carve-outs sit on the same structure, so your desk is subject to the same rule as the channel. A rule the manufacturer exempts itself from is not a rule a partner will trust.

faqs.q: Can I quote against an exclusivity when I need to?
faqs.a: Yes, with an override by an authorised user, and the override is recorded with who, when and why. On Enterprise it also lands in the immutable audit log. What we will not do is let it happen silently.

faqs.q: Does this set dealer pricing?
faqs.a: No. What a partner pays sits on a contract price list. Exclusivity answers who may sell, pricing answers at what price, and keeping them separate stops a change to one quietly changing the other.
