items.name: Territory management
items.metaDescription: Define territories up to seven levels deep, assign accounts and owners, and report coverage and performance at any level. In development, target Wave 1 M4.
items.lead: Country, region, state, zone, city, cluster, route. Seven levels because that is how a real distribution structure is actually shaped.
items.answer: Territory management in KanchanFlow defines a sales geography up to seven levels deep, assigns accounts and owners at any level, and reports coverage and performance by node. It is roughly 30 percent complete, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 4. Starter keeps a flat territory list; the hierarchy is a Professional and Enterprise capability.
summary: A growing manufacturer's sales geography stops fitting in a flat list quickly. You have regions with managers, states with representatives, cities with dealers and routes for field calls, and each level needs an owner, a target and a coverage measure. Most shops keep this in a spreadsheet nobody updated after the last reorganisation.

The hierarchy holds up to seven levels so the structure in the system matches the structure on the ground. Accounts and dealers are assigned to nodes, ownership rolls up, and performance and coverage report at any level. When territories change — and they do — accounts move with a record of when and why.

capabilities.title: Seven levels of hierarchy
capabilities.body: Enough depth for country, region, state, zone, city, cluster and route without forcing a real structure into three levels and losing the shape of it.

capabilities.title: Ownership at every level
capabilities.body: A node has an owner, and ownership rolls up. A regional manager sees everything under them without being individually assigned to each account.

capabilities.title: Account and dealer assignment
capabilities.body: Direct accounts and channel partners both sit in the territory structure, so the coverage picture includes the channel rather than only direct business.

capabilities.title: Coverage reporting by node
capabilities.body: Which accounts in this territory have been visited, quoted or ordered from in the period, and which have been left alone. The untouched list is the useful half.

capabilities.title: Reassignment with a history
capabilities.body: When a territory changes, accounts move and the change is recorded. Historical performance stays attributable to whoever actually held the territory at the time.

capabilities.title: Lead and enquiry routing by geography
capabilities.body: New enquiries route to the owner of the territory the buyer sits in, so an IndiaMART or web enquiry from a city you cover reaches the person who already knows that market rather than a central queue.

howItWorks.name: Design the hierarchy
howItWorks.text: Build the levels that match your business. Not every branch needs the same depth — a dense region may run to seven levels while another stops at three.

howItWorks.name: Assign owners
howItWorks.text: Give each node an owner. Ownership rolls up automatically so managers see their whole area without per-account assignment.

howItWorks.name: Place accounts and dealers
howItWorks.text: Assign direct accounts and channel partners to territory nodes, individually or in bulk by geography.

howItWorks.name: Work the territory

howItWorks.name: Report at any level
howItWorks.text: Coverage, quoting activity and order value report at any node, rolled up or drilled into.

items.name: Sales visit intelligence
items.h1: Sales visit intelligence — voice to CRM
items.metaDescription: Dictate what happened after a customer visit and have it become structured notes, follow-up tasks and record updates for you to approve. Target Wave 1 M5.
items.lead: Talk for ninety seconds in the car park. Get structured notes, follow-up tasks and the next step on the record — with a person confirming before anything is saved.
items.answer: Sales visit intelligence turns a spoken debrief after a customer visit into structured notes, follow-up tasks and record updates in the KanchanFlow RFQ-to-Order CRM, presented for human confirmation before saving. It is roughly 40 percent complete, targeted at Wave 1 Milestone 5, and it runs against your AI credit allowance.
summary: The gap between a good sales call and a useful CRM record is a typing job that happens at nine at night, if it happens. What is lost is not the headline — it is the detail: the engineer's objection to the surface finish, the competitor they mentioned, the date the programme actually starts.

The work in progress lets the salesperson speak the debrief into the mobile app while it is fresh. The transcript is turned into structured output — what was discussed, who was there, objections raised, next steps with dates — and shown for confirmation. Nothing is written to the record until a person approves it, in line with our approval-first stance on AI.

capabilities.title: Voice capture in the field
capabilities.body: Record the debrief in the mobile app immediately after the visit, when the detail is still there. Ninety seconds of speech beats a paragraph typed three days later.

capabilities.title: Structured output, not a wall of text
capabilities.body: Discussion points, attendees, objections, competitor mentions and next steps are separated into fields, because a transcript nobody re-reads is not a record.

capabilities.title: Follow-up tasks with dates
capabilities.body: 'Send revised quote by Friday' becomes a task with an owner and a due date, rather than a sentence buried in a note.

capabilities.title: Confirmation before saving
capabilities.body: The extracted structure is shown next to the transcript for the salesperson to correct and approve. Nothing reaches the record unconfirmed.

capabilities.title: Attached to the visit and the account
capabilities.body: The confirmed summary attaches to the visit record and the customer timeline, where the next person to open the account will find it.

howItWorks.name: Finish the visit and check out
howItWorks.text: The visit is already checked in with GPS, so the debrief attaches to a known visit at a known customer.

howItWorks.name: Speak the debrief
howItWorks.text: Record in the mobile app. Talk the way you would tell a colleague what happened — the structuring is the software's job, not yours.

howItWorks.name: Transcription and extraction run
howItWorks.text: The recording is transcribed and structured. Meeting summarisation consumes three credits up to thirty minutes and six credits from thirty to sixty.

howItWorks.name: Confirm or correct
howItWorks.text: The structured output appears next to the transcript. Fix anything wrong, then approve. Nothing saves before that.

howItWorks.name: Tasks and updates are created
howItWorks.text: Follow-up tasks are created with dates and owners, and the summary attaches to the visit and the customer timeline.

items.name: Purchase order OCR
items.metaDescription: Read a customer purchase order PDF into structured order lines and check them against the quote they came from, with human confirmation. Target Wave 1 M4.
items.lead: The customer's PO arrives as a PDF from their ERP. Read it, match it against the quote, and flag the line where the price does not agree — before you accept the order.
items.answer: Purchase order OCR reads a customer's PO document into structured lines inside the KanchanFlow RFQ-to-Order CRM and compares them against the quote the order came from. It is in development with a Wave 1 Milestone 4 target, runs against your AI credit allowance at three credits per page, and always asks a person to confirm before the order is created.
summary: A customer PO is a legal document that frequently disagrees with the quote it is answering. The quantity is different, the price is from a superseded revision, the delivery date is two weeks earlier, or the terms have quietly become net sixty. Somebody has to read the PDF against the quote, and in most shops that somebody is doing it at speed.

The work in progress extracts the header and lines from the PO — buyer, PO number, dates, part numbers, quantities, prices and terms — and puts them next to the quote for comparison. Differences are highlighted rather than accepted. The order is created only after a person confirms, and any accepted difference is recorded on the order.

capabilities.title: Header and line extraction
capabilities.body: PO number, buyer, order date, required date, ship-to, payment terms and every line with part number, quantity and price come out of the document as fields, not as a scanned image in an attachment folder.

capabilities.title: Comparison against the quote
capabilities.body: Extracted lines are matched to the quote they answer and differences in price, quantity, lead time and terms are highlighted individually.

capabilities.title: Confirmation before the order exists
capabilities.body: Nothing becomes an order on the strength of an extraction. A person reviews the comparison, accepts or queries the differences, and then the order is created.

capabilities.title: Accepted differences recorded
capabilities.body: Where you accept a customer's changed price or date, the acceptance is recorded on the order against the original quote figure, so the variance is visible later.

capabilities.title: The PO document stays attached
capabilities.body: The original PDF remains attached to the order. The extraction is a convenience; the customer's document is the evidence.

howItWorks.name: The PO arrives
howItWorks.text: Upload the PDF, or let it arrive on the email thread attached to the quote. It is stored against the quote before anything is read.

howItWorks.name: Extraction runs
howItWorks.text: Header and line data are read from the document at the published PO OCR weight of three AI credits per page.

howItWorks.name: Compare against the quote
howItWorks.text: Extracted lines are matched to quote lines. Price, quantity, date and terms differences are highlighted with both values shown side by side.

howItWorks.name: A person decides
howItWorks.text: Accept the differences, query them with the buyer, or reject the PO. Nothing proceeds on the extraction alone.

howItWorks.name: The order is created
howItWorks.text: On confirmation the order is created with the customer PO number attached, and any accepted variance recorded against the quoted figure.

items.name: Sample tracking
items.metaDescription: Track a sample from request through quotation, production, dispatch, customer trial and approval across nine stages, with the decision recorded on it.
items.lead: Samples are where new business is won and where follow-up dies. Nine stages, an owner at each, and a recorded verdict at the end instead of silence.
items.answer: Sample tracking follows a customer sample through nine stages in the KanchanFlow RFQ-to-Order CRM — from request to approval or rejection — with an owner and a date at each stage. It is in development with a Wave 1 Milestone 4 target. Starter carries a five-stage lifecycle; the full nine-stage version is Professional and Enterprise.
summary: Every job shop makes samples, and almost none of them track what happened to them. A sample is requested, quoted, made, shipped, and then it goes quiet. Three months later nobody knows whether it was approved, rejected, or is still sitting on a shelf in the customer's lab, and the salesperson has stopped asking.

The nine-stage lifecycle makes each transition a recorded event with an owner and a date: requested, quoted, approved to make, in production, quality checked, dispatched, received, under trial, and finally approved or rejected with a reason. The stages that stall are visible, and the ones that end in rejection produce a reason you can act on.

capabilities.title: Nine stages with owners and dates
capabilities.body: Each stage has a named owner and a date it was entered, so a sample sitting in quality for three weeks is visible as a fact rather than as a suspicion.

capabilities.title: Recorded verdict with a reason
capabilities.body: Approved or rejected, with a reason — dimensional, finish, material, commercial. Rejection reasons across a year are the most useful quality data most shops never collect.

capabilities.title: Linked to the RFQ and the quote
capabilities.body: Samples belong to the enquiry that prompted them, so the eventual production order can be traced back through the sample to the original RFQ.

capabilities.title: Stalled sample alerts

capabilities.title: Cost of samples

howItWorks.name: Quote and internal approval

howItWorks.name: Production and quality

howItWorks.name: Dispatch and receipt
howItWorks.text: Dispatched with a reference, then marked received. The clock on the customer's trial starts from a known date rather than a guess.

howItWorks.name: Trial and verdict
howItWorks.text: Under trial with the customer, then approved or rejected with a reason. An approved sample is the trigger for the production quote.

items.name: Immutable audit log
items.h1: Immutable audit log for compliance-driven manufacturers
items.metaDescription: An append-only record of who changed what and when across quotes, orders, approvals and pricing, exportable for audit. In development, target Wave 1 M5.
items.lead: We are the CRM, not the certifier. What we can give a compliance-driven shop is a record of every change that cannot be quietly edited afterwards.
items.answer: The immutable audit log is an append-only record of every material change in KanchanFlow — quote pricing, approvals, order amendments, permission changes — with the user, timestamp and before-and-after values. It is in development for Wave 1 Milestone 5 and is a Professional and Enterprise capability, with the compliance dashboard on Enterprise.
summary: Shops working to AS9100, ITAR or a customer's supplier quality requirement get asked the same question in every audit: show me who changed this and when. A CRM whose history can be edited cannot answer that question, and a screenshot of a record is not evidence of anything. An auditor wants a log, produced from the system, that nobody could have edited.

The audit log is append-only. Entries are written when a change happens and cannot be modified or deleted from the interface, including by an administrator. Each entry carries the user, the timestamp, the record, the field and the values before and after. On Enterprise the compliance dashboard summarises the log and the export produces the evidence pack an auditor asks for.

capabilities.title: Append-only by construction
capabilities.body: Entries cannot be edited or deleted from the application, by any role including administrators. An audit log with an edit button is not an audit log.

capabilities.title: Before-and-after values
capabilities.body: Each entry records the field, the previous value and the new value, so a price change from $412 to $388 reads as exactly that rather than as 'quote updated'.

capabilities.title: Coverage of the decisions that matter
capabilities.body: Quote pricing and revisions, approval decisions and overrides, order amendments, credit limit changes, permission and role changes, and eSign and IRN events.

capabilities.title: Export for auditors
capabilities.body: Filter by record, user, date range or event type and export the result, so responding to an audit request is a query rather than a fortnight of screenshots.

capabilities.title: Compliance dashboard on Enterprise
capabilities.body: A summary view over the log — override frequency, approval bypasses, permission changes — for the person who has to sign the supplier quality questionnaire.

howItWorks.name: Enable it on the workspace
howItWorks.text: The log is switched on for the workspace on Professional and Enterprise. Once on, it records continuously without per-record configuration.

howItWorks.name: Changes are written as they happen
howItWorks.text: Every material change writes an entry with the user, the timestamp, the record, the field and both values. Nothing depends on someone remembering to note it.

howItWorks.name: Read it from the record
howItWorks.text: Any quote or order shows its own change history in place, so the common question — what happened to this job — is answered without a separate report.

howItWorks.name: Query across the workspace
howItWorks.text: Filter by user, date range, record type or event type when the question is broader than a single record.

howItWorks.name: Export the evidence
howItWorks.text: Produce a filtered export for an auditor or a customer's supplier quality team, with the entries in their original form.

faqs.a: No, and we will never say it does. We are the CRM, not the certifier. What we provide is the immutable change record a compliance-driven manufacturer is asked to produce.

faqs.q: Can an administrator delete an entry?
faqs.a: No. The log is append-only from the application for every role. That property is the entire value of the feature.

faqs.q: What is recorded?
faqs.a: Quote pricing and revisions, approval decisions and overrides, order amendments, credit limit changes, permission and role changes, and signature and IRN events.

faqs.a: Professional and Enterprise. Enterprise adds the compliance dashboard over the top of the log.

faqs.a: The report is available to Enterprise customers. SOC 2 Type II is an audited control of ours; it is not a statement about your shop's certifications.

items.name: MSMED 43B(h) tracker
items.subhead: For USA manufacturers with India operations, India-based contract customers, or manufacturers exporting to India.
items.metaDescription: Track payments to registered micro and small suppliers against the 45-day Section 43B(h) window, with exposure visible before year end. Target Wave 1 M3.
items.lead: A payment to a registered micro or small supplier that crosses forty-five days is disallowed as a deduction. This counts the days while you can still do something about it.
items.answer: The MSMED Section 43B(h) tracker watches payments to registered micro and small enterprise suppliers against the statutory 45-day window inside KanchanFlow, and shows the deduction exposure building before year end. It is in development with a Wave 1 Milestone 3 target and, like every India regulatory feature here, is included on every tier.
summary: Section 43B(h) of India's Income Tax Act disallows a deduction for amounts owed to registered micro and small enterprises that are not paid within forty-five days. The consequence is not a fine, it is a larger tax bill, and it usually arrives as a surprise from the auditor months after the payments were missed.

The tracker classifies suppliers by their Udyam registration, counts days from the acceptance of goods or services, and shows which invoices are approaching or past the window along with the deduction exposure attached to them. The point is to make the number visible in week five, not in the following October.

capabilities.title: Supplier classification by Udyam registration
capabilities.body: Suppliers carry their registration and classification — micro, small, medium or unregistered — because the rule only bites for registered micro and small enterprises.

capabilities.title: Day counting from the right date
capabilities.body: The clock runs from acceptance of goods or services, not from the invoice date or the date somebody entered it. Getting the start date wrong makes the whole count wrong.

capabilities.title: Approaching and breached buckets
capabilities.body: Invoices within the window, approaching the limit and past it are separated, so the list you act on is short and specific.

capabilities.title: Deduction exposure figure
capabilities.body: The rupee value of amounts that would be disallowed if unpaid at year end, rather than a count of invoices. That figure is what gets attention.

capabilities.title: Advanced exposure calculator on Enterprise
capabilities.body: Enterprise adds scenario analysis across entities — what the exposure becomes if a payment run slips a fortnight — on top of the same underlying data.

howItWorks.name: Classify your suppliers
howItWorks.text: Record each supplier's Udyam registration and classification. GSTIN validation on the vendor record supports this, and unregistered suppliers are marked as such.

howItWorks.name: Record acceptance
howItWorks.text: The day count starts from acceptance of goods or services. Recording that date is the step most manual processes skip, and it is the one that matters.

howItWorks.name: Watch the buckets
howItWorks.text: Invoices to registered micro and small suppliers sit in within-window, approaching and breached buckets, updated daily.

howItWorks.name: Act before day forty-five
howItWorks.text: The approaching bucket is a payment run instruction. Acting there is the whole purpose; the breached bucket is already a cost.

howItWorks.name: See the exposure
howItWorks.text: The running deduction exposure shows what would be disallowed at year end on current behaviour, so the conversation happens in month three rather than month eleven.

tierAvailability.professional: Included. Same tracker as Starter.
tierAvailability.enterprise: Included, plus the advanced exposure calculator and multi-entity scenario analysis.

faqs.q: Why does a USA-focused CRM track an Indian tax rule?
faqs.a: Because USA manufacturers with India operations or India-based contract suppliers are exposed to it, and the exposure is invisible until an auditor raises it.

faqs.q: Is it gated by tier?
faqs.a: No. The 43B(h) tracker, GST invoicing, IRN generation and GSTIN validation are on every tier including Starter. India regulatory features are never a pricing lever here.

faqs.q: Where does the 45-day count start?
faqs.a: From acceptance of the goods or services. Counting from the invoice date is the common mistake and it produces a comfortable number that is wrong.

faqs.q: Does it apply to every supplier?
faqs.a: No, only to suppliers registered as micro or small enterprises. Classification comes from their Udyam registration, which is why supplier classification is step one.

faqs.q: Is this tax advice?
faqs.a: No. We track the window and show exposure. The treatment in your return is your accountant's determination, and we do not pretend otherwise.

items.name: Revenue leakage dashboard
items.metaDescription: Six metrics showing where revenue leaks: unquoted RFQs, expired quotes, unfollowed quotes, below-floor lines, unbilled dispatches and overdue receivables.
items.lead: Six places money leaves a job shop quietly. Not a chart wall — six numbers, each with the list of records underneath it that you can act on today.
items.answer: The revenue leakage dashboard surfaces six specific ways money is lost in a manufacturing business — enquiries never quoted, quotes never followed, quotes expired, lines below margin floor, dispatches never invoiced and receivables past terms. It is in development for Wave 1 Milestone 4; Starter carries three metrics, Professional and Enterprise the full six.
summary: Shops lose money in ways that never appear on a profit and loss statement as a line item. An enquiry that was never quoted is not a loss anyone records. A dispatch that was never invoiced looks like a slow month. A quote that expired unopened is filed as a loss to a competitor who never even bid.

The dashboard names six of these and puts a number and a list against each. The list is the point: every metric drills straight into the records behind it, so the dashboard produces work rather than a discussion. On Starter it shows three metrics; the full six are on Professional and Enterprise.

capabilities.title: Enquiries received but never quoted
capabilities.body: The RFQs that came in and never produced a quote or a recorded no-quote decision. In most shops this is the largest and least visible number on the page.

capabilities.title: Quotes sent but never followed up
capabilities.body: Quotes past their follow-up date with no logged call, message or email. The Quote Follow-Up Agent drafts the chase; this is the list it works from.

capabilities.title: Quotes expired without an outcome
capabilities.body: Quotes that passed their validity date with no win, loss or revision recorded. An expired quote with no outcome is a sale nobody closed and nobody learned from.

capabilities.title: Lines sent below the margin floor
capabilities.body: Quoted lines priced under the applicable floor, with and without approval, grouped by customer and product family so a pattern of concession is visible.

capabilities.title: Dispatched but not invoiced
capabilities.body: Order lines where goods have shipped and no invoice has been raised. This is real money already spent on material and labour, sitting uninvoiced.

capabilities.title: Receivables past terms
capabilities.body: Invoiced value past due by aging bucket, tied to the salesperson who owns the account rather than only to the finance team.

howItWorks.name: The dashboard reads live records
howItWorks.text: Nothing here is a separate data entry exercise. Every metric is computed from the RFQs, quotes, orders and invoices already in the system.

howItWorks.name: Set your thresholds
howItWorks.text: Follow-up interval, margin floor and payment terms come from your own configuration, so the numbers reflect your standards rather than a default.

howItWorks.name: Read the six numbers
howItWorks.text: Each metric shows a count and a value. Value is what makes the ranking honest — forty small leaks may matter less than two large ones.

howItWorks.name: Drill into the list
howItWorks.text: Every metric opens the records behind it. The dashboard's output is a work list, not a chart to screenshot for a meeting.

howItWorks.name: Work it and watch it move
howItWorks.text: The numbers update as the records change, so the effect of a week of follow-up calls is visible rather than assumed.

faqs.a: In development with a Wave 1 Milestone 4 target. It depends on the RFQ record and the margin guardrails, which are being built for the same and adjacent milestones.

items.name: Owner command centre
items.metaDescription: Six panels an owner actually opens: quote pipeline, order book, approvals waiting, leakage, cash and channel health. In development, target Wave 1 M4.
items.lead: One screen for the person who signs the cheques. Six panels, each answering a question an owner asks on a Monday, each opening into the records underneath.
items.answer: The manufacturing owner command centre is a six-panel home screen in the KanchanFlow RFQ-to-Order CRM covering quote pipeline, order book, approvals waiting, revenue leakage, cash position and channel health. It is in development for Wave 1 Milestone 4. Starter carries a simplified version; the full six panels are on Professional and Enterprise.
summary: The owner of a fifty-person shop does not want a CRM. They want the four or five things they would otherwise ask four or five people for, on one screen, correct, without a meeting. Everything else in the product exists so this screen can be accurate. If the underlying records are wrong, no dashboard on top of them can be right.

Six panels: what is quoted and where it stands, what is on order and when it ships, what needs the owner's decision today, where revenue is leaking, what cash is coming and what is overdue, and how the dealer channel is behaving. Every panel opens into records, because a number without a list is only a mood.

capabilities.title: Quote pipeline
capabilities.body: Open quote value by stage and age, with win rate over the trailing period. Quotes older than your follow-up threshold are called out rather than averaged away.

capabilities.title: Order book
capabilities.body: Booked value, what is dispatched, what is outstanding and what is at risk on delivery date. This is the panel the plant manager will read over your shoulder.

capabilities.title: Approvals waiting on you
capabilities.body: Discounts, below-floor margins and terms exceptions waiting on the owner, with the cost buildup and customer history attached, approvable from the phone.

capabilities.title: Revenue leakage summary
capabilities.body: The headline figures from the leakage dashboard — unquoted enquiries, unfollowed quotes, unbilled dispatches — with the full dashboard one click away.

capabilities.title: Cash position
capabilities.body: Invoiced and outstanding by aging bucket, expected receipts, and customers at or over their credit limit. Aging and pipeline on one screen is a rarer thing than it should be.

capabilities.title: Channel health
capabilities.body: Dealer ordering behaviour, partners past their expected reorder date, and channel value against direct. Only meaningful if you sell through a channel, and hidden if you do not.

howItWorks.name: Drill into anything
howItWorks.text: Each panel opens the records behind it. The screen exists to start work, not to be screenshotted into a board pack.

howItWorks.text: The same six panels appear in the mobile app, which is where most owners will actually read them.

items.name: AI drawing OCR
items.h1: AI drawing OCR for GD&T and tolerances
items.metaDescription: Not built. We are exploring with partners whether GD&T symbols and tolerance callouts can be read from a drawing accurately enough to quote from.
items.lead: This feature does not exist. We are in partner exploration on whether GD&T and tolerance extraction can be made accurate enough to be worth trusting, and we have no committed date.
items.answer: AI drawing OCR for GD&T and tolerances is not built. KanchanFlow is exploring with partners whether geometric dimensioning and tolerancing symbols can be read from a drawing reliably enough to price from. It is a Wave 3 exploration with no committed date, and nothing on this page is available to buy today.
summary: We are stating this plainly because the alternative is worse: this feature does not exist, is not in development, and has no date. It is on our public list because we are genuinely investigating it, not because we intend to sell it to you this year. Publishing an exploration honestly is the only way a roadmap stays worth reading.

The problem is harder than general document OCR. GD&T is a symbolic language layered on geometry, where a feature control frame's meaning depends on the datum structure elsewhere on the print. Reading the symbols is achievable; reading them correctly enough that an estimator would price a job from the output without checking is not something we can currently claim.

capabilities.title: What we are exploring
capabilities.body: Whether feature control frames, datum references and tolerance callouts can be extracted from a drawing with enough accuracy and enough confidence scoring to be useful to an estimator.

capabilities.title: Why partners
capabilities.body: The specialist capability here sits with vendors who have worked on engineering drawing interpretation for years. We are more likely to integrate one than to build our own from nothing.

capabilities.title: The accuracy bar we would need
capabilities.body: An extraction an estimator has to verify symbol by symbol saves nobody any time. The bar is confident extraction with honest uncertainty flagging, and we are not near it.

capabilities.title: What exists instead today
capabilities.body: Drawing revision management with AI spec extraction, in development for Wave 1 Milestone 3, reads material, finish and general tolerance for human confirmation. That is a much narrower and more achievable claim.

capabilities.title: What would have to be true first
capabilities.body: Extraction accurate enough to price from, confidence reporting honest enough that an estimator knows which callouts to check, and a cost per drawing low enough to be worth the credits. None of those three are settled.

howItWorks.name: Nothing works yet
howItWorks.text: There is no implementation to describe. This section will be written when there is something real to describe, and not before.

howItWorks.name: We are assessing partners
howItWorks.text: We are evaluating specialist drawing interpretation vendors against real customer prints rather than against their demo sets.

howItWorks.name: We are defining the accuracy bar
howItWorks.text: Establishing what accuracy and confidence reporting would need to look like for a shop to use the output at all.

howItWorks.name: If it clears the bar, we will schedule it
howItWorks.text: At that point it would get a wave, a milestone and a status change on this page. Until then it stays here as an exploration.

faqs.a: There is no committed date. It is a Wave 3 partner exploration. If that changes, this page changes and it will appear in the changelog.

faqs.a: Probably not. The specialist capability sits with vendors who have worked on this for years, and integrating one is the more honest path than claiming we can do it from scratch.

items.lead: This feature does not exist. The intent is to open a customer's STEP, IGES or DWG file in the browser from the quote. Wave 2, indicative Q2 2027 — direction, not a commitment.
items.answer: An embedded CAD viewer for STEP, IGES and DWG files is not built. The intent is that anyone quoting in KanchanFlow could open the customer's model from the quote record without a CAD seat. It is Wave 2 with an indicative Q2 2027 direction, which is not a commitment and not a date you should plan around.
summary: Today you can attach STEP, IGES and DWG files to a quote and they travel with it — the file management works. What you cannot do is look at them without opening a CAD package, which means the estimator, the inside sales person and the owner are all dependent on whoever has a licence.

The planned viewer would render the attached model in the browser with basic measurement and section views. We are publishing an indicative Q2 2027 for Wave 2 because we publish one quarter out at most as a commitment and everything beyond that is direction. Nothing here is available now. Treat the quarter as a signal of intent and nothing more than that.

capabilities.title: Basic measurement

capabilities.title: Viewing without a CAD seat

items.name: Customer-exclusive parts
items.metaDescription: Not built. A planned ownership flag for parts made only for one customer — their tooling, their print, never quoted to anyone else. Wave 2, no date.
items.lead: This feature does not exist. The intent is to mark a part as belonging to one customer — their tooling, their print, their part number — so it can never be quoted to anyone else. Wave 2, no committed date.
items.answer: Customer-exclusive parts are not built in KanchanFlow. The intent is an ownership flag on the part record marking tooling, drawings and geometry as belonging to one customer, excluded from similar-part search for every other account. It is a Wave 2 item with no committed date, and nothing on this page is available today.
summary: Almost every contract manufacturer holds parts that are not theirs. The customer paid for the tooling, the print carries their title block and their drawing number, and the part exists only because they asked for it. The obligation that comes with that is usually written into a supply agreement in one sentence and then managed entirely by the memory of whoever has been at the shop the longest. It survives until that person retires, or until a new estimator pulls up a similar job to price a new enquiry and finds a fixture, a routing and a price that belong to somebody else's customer.

The exposure is not theoretical. A shop quoting a new prospect off the routing of a proprietary part is quoting somebody else's development spend, and a print with another customer's title block sent out as a reference is a confidentiality breach with a name and a date attached to it. Neither is malicious. Both come from a system that treats every part in the database as equally available to whoever is quoting today.

What is planned is an ownership flag on the part record and the consequences that follow from it. The part is owned by one account. Its drawings are marked confidential to that account. Its tooling is recorded as customer-owned, with the tool number, who paid for it and where it physically sits. And the part is excluded from similar-part search results for every other customer, so it cannot be used as a reference price or a routing template for anyone else. The exclusion is the part that matters most, because search is exactly where the accident happens.

The interesting case is a second customer arriving with the same geometry, which happens more often than people expect — two OEMs buying from the same design house, or a part that is genuinely commodity apart from the print it arrived on. The intent is not to refuse the work. It is to make sure the second quote is estimated from scratch, on the second customer's own drawing, without inheriting the first customer's routing, tooling or price. The estimator would be told that a match exists and that it is restricted, without being shown the restricted record. Knowing that a similar part is off limits is useful. Seeing the part you are not allowed to see is not.

Nothing above is built. There is no ownership flag, no confidentiality marking on drawings and no search exclusion today, on any tier. It sits in Wave 2 with no committed date, and we are not going to publish a quarter for it just to make the page look decisive. What exists now is described in the next section, honestly.

capabilities.title: What works today
capabilities.body: Parts, drawings and revisions attach to the customer they were quoted for, and role-based permissions control who inside your shop can open a record at all. What does not exist is any concept of a part being owned by a customer, or of a drawing being confidential to one account.

capabilities.title: Intended: an ownership flag on the part
capabilities.body: A part marked as belonging to one account, so the relationship is a property of the record rather than something two people remember. Everything else in this list follows from that one flag.

capabilities.title: Intended: confidentiality on the drawing
capabilities.body: Prints carrying another company's title block marked as confidential to that customer, so they cannot be attached to a quote for a different account or sent in a share link by accident.

capabilities.title: Intended: customer-owned tooling recorded
capabilities.body: Tool number, who paid for it, where it is stored and which parts run on it. Customer-owned tooling is an asset you hold on somebody else's behalf, and it should be findable when they ask for it back.

capabilities.title: Intended: exclusion from similar-part search
capabilities.body: The similar-part search that Professional and Enterprise run on AI credits would skip restricted parts for every account except the owner. Search is where the accident actually happens, so this is the part of the idea that carries the weight.

capabilities.title: Intended: a restricted-match signal without disclosure
capabilities.body: An estimator would be told that a match exists and is restricted, and shown nothing about it. Enough to stop them assuming the part is new, not enough to leak what it is.

capabilities.title: What it would never be
capabilities.body: Not a legal NDA register, not an ITAR or export-control regime, and not a substitute for the confidentiality clause in your supply agreement. Enterprise carries ITAR handling and an immutable audit log for controlled work; this would be a commercial hygiene flag, nothing more.

howItWorks.name: Nothing works yet
howItWorks.text: There is no ownership flag, no drawing confidentiality marking and no search exclusion. A part quoted for one customer is visible to anyone in your workspace with permission to see parts at all.

howItWorks.name: What you can do in the meantime
howItWorks.text: Use role-based permissions to limit who can reach part and drawing records, keep customer-owned tooling in a named list somebody actually maintains, and make the confidentiality rule an explicit line in your estimator onboarding rather than folklore.

howItWorks.name: Why it sits in Wave 2
howItWorks.text: Wave 1 is the RFQ record, the cost buildup, approvals and the dealer channel. Each of those changes what a shop can do. This changes what a shop can accidentally do, which matters, but not before the work that earns the quote.

howItWorks.name: What would have to be decided first
howItWorks.text: Whether ownership is a flag on the part or a relationship that can cover several accounts, how a second customer's identical geometry is handled in the data model, and what an estimator is allowed to be told about a restricted match. Those are design questions we have not settled.

howItWorks.name: The status would change here first
howItWorks.text: If it enters development it gets a milestone and a progress figure on this page, and a changelog entry when it ships. Until then it stays planned, with no date and no index.

faqs.q: Can I mark a part as belonging to one customer today?
faqs.a: No. There is no ownership flag on any tier. Parts and drawings attach to the customer they were quoted for, and role-based permissions control who can open a record, but nothing stops a part from being used as a reference for another account.

faqs.q: What happens when a second customer asks for the same geometry?
faqs.a: Today, nothing special happens — and that is the problem the feature exists to solve. The intent is that the second quote is estimated from scratch on the second customer's own drawing, without inheriting the first customer's routing, tooling or price, and that the estimator is told a restricted match exists without being shown it.

faqs.q: Would restricted parts still appear in similar-part search?
faqs.a: For the owning customer, yes. For everyone else, no. Search is where the mistake actually happens, so exclusion is the centre of the idea rather than an extra on top of it.

faqs.q: Is there a date?
faqs.a: No, and we are not going to invent one. It is Wave 2 with no committed date. We publish one quarter out as a commitment and label everything beyond that as direction; this does not have even that yet.

faqs.q: Does this cover ITAR or export-controlled work?
faqs.a: No. ITAR handling, PPAP, USMCA and Buy America modules are Enterprise capabilities, and the immutable audit log is what compliance-driven shops rely on. This would be a commercial confidentiality flag, not an export-control regime, and we are the CRM rather than the certifier.

faqs.q: How do I protect customer tooling in the meantime?
faqs.a: Keep a maintained list of customer-owned tools with the tool number, the owner and the location, restrict part and drawing access by role, and write the confidentiality rule into estimator onboarding. None of that is as good as a flag on the record, and we would rather say so than sell you one that does not exist.

items.name: PPAP for automotive
items.metaDescription: Not built. A planned PPAP submission package workflow for automotive tier suppliers. Wave 3, H2 2027 direction, no committed date, not available today.
items.lead: This feature does not exist. Assembling and tracking a PPAP submission is a real need for automotive tier suppliers and it is on our Wave 3 list with no committed date.
items.answer: PPAP for automotive tier suppliers is not built. The intent is to assemble and track a Production Part Approval Process submission package against a customer part inside KanchanFlow. It is a Wave 3 item with an H2 2027 direction and no committed date, and it is not something you can buy or use today.
summary: PPAP is the automotive industry's evidence package that a part can be made repeatably to specification: the control plan, the process flow, the FMEA, the dimensional results, the material certifications and the part submission warrant, assembled and submitted to the customer for approval. It is a substantial documentation exercise, and it is repeated for every new part number.

For a supplier into an automotive tier, assembling that package is a fortnight of work per part and tracking its approval state across dozens of parts is a spreadsheet job. We think a CRM that already holds the part, the drawing revision and the customer relationship is a reasonable place to track it. We have not built any of it.

capabilities.title: What is intended
capabilities.body: Track a PPAP submission per customer part: the submission level, the documents required, which are complete, and the customer's approval state.

capabilities.title: Linked to the part and drawing revision
capabilities.body: A PPAP is against a specific drawing revision. The link to revision management is the reason this belongs near the CRM rather than in a shared folder.

capabilities.title: What we would not do
capabilities.body: We would not generate the FMEA or the control plan. Those are engineering documents produced by your quality team; we would track and package them.

capabilities.title: Enterprise scope
capabilities.body: If built, this would be an Enterprise capability alongside ITAR, USMCA and Buy America, matching how those compliance modules are tiered today.

capabilities.title: What we would need from you
capabilities.body: The control plan, process flow, FMEA and dimensional results are produced by your quality team. Any workflow we build tracks completeness and submission state against a drawing revision; it does not author engineering documents.

howItWorks.name: Nothing works yet

items.name: USMCA origin tracking
items.h1: USMCA origin tracking with auto-generated certificates
items.metaDescription: Not built. Planned origin tracking and certification for USMCA preferential treatment on cross-border shipments. Wave 3, H2 2027 direction, no committed date.
items.lead: This feature does not exist. Tracking regional value content and producing a certification of origin is on our Wave 3 list, with an H2 2027 direction and no committed date.
items.answer: USMCA origin tracking with auto-generated certificates is not built. The intent is to track regional value content on parts and produce a certification of origin for shipments claiming preferential treatment under the agreement. It is Wave 3 with an H2 2027 direction, no committed date, and nothing here is available today.
summary: Manufacturers shipping between the United States, Mexico and Canada can claim preferential tariff treatment under USMCA if the goods meet the rules of origin, and the certification is a producer statement with real consequences if it is wrong. Most shops handle it with a template document and an anxious conversation with a customs broker.

The intent would be to carry origin data on the part — material origin, processing performed, regional value content — and produce the certification from that record rather than from a re-typed template. We have built none of it, and until we do this page exists to say so. Publishing an empty page beats publishing a page that implies a capability.

capabilities.title: What is intended
capabilities.body: Origin attributes on the part and its material, a regional value content calculation, and a certification of origin generated from the underlying record rather than typed fresh each time.

capabilities.title: Blanket and shipment certifications
capabilities.body: Both patterns are used in practice — a blanket period certification and a per-shipment one — and both would need supporting.

capabilities.title: Traceability to the evidence
capabilities.body: A certification is a statement you sign. It should point at the material origin records and processing evidence that support it, which is the CRM's contribution.

capabilities.title: Enterprise scope
capabilities.body: If built, it would sit with ITAR, PPAP and Buy America as an Enterprise compliance module, matching the current tiering of that group.

capabilities.title: Why it is not built yet
capabilities.body: Rules of origin vary by tariff classification, so the work starts with classification rather than with a certificate template. That is a larger piece of scope than the certificate itself, and we have not done it.

howItWorks.name: Nothing works yet
howItWorks.text: There is no origin tracking or certificate generation in the product. This is intent, not capability.

howItWorks.name: The rules are part-specific
howItWorks.text: Rules of origin vary by tariff classification, so any real implementation starts with classification, which is work we have not scoped.

howItWorks.name: It depends on material tracking
howItWorks.text: Material tracking is live and would be the source of origin data, but the origin attributes themselves do not exist on it yet.

howItWorks.name: Status would change here first
howItWorks.text: Entering development would put a milestone and a progress figure on this page.

howItWorks.name: What to do in the meantime
howItWorks.text: Keep the origin determination with your customs broker and keep the supporting material certificates attached to the order in material tracking, which is live today and holds the mill certs the determination rests on.

items.name: Buy America calculator
items.metaDescription: Not built. A planned domestic content percentage calculator for Buy America and Build America Buy America rules. Wave 3, H2 2027, no committed date.
items.lead: This feature does not exist. Calculating and evidencing domestic content percentage for federally funded work is on our Wave 3 list, with no committed date.
items.answer: The Buy America content-percentage calculator is not built. The intent is to calculate domestic content percentage across a part's material and processing and hold the evidence behind the figure. It is a Wave 3 item with an H2 2027 direction and no committed date, and none of it is available in KanchanFlow today.
summary: Manufacturers supplying into federally funded infrastructure work face domestic content requirements, and the certifications that go with them are backed by a percentage somebody has to calculate and defend. In most shops that calculation lives in a spreadsheet built once for one contract and adapted under pressure ever since. Nobody wants to defend that spreadsheet in front of a contracting officer.

The intent is to compute the percentage from material and processing records already in the system and keep the supporting evidence attached to the figure. We have not built it, and putting a mock screenshot on this page would misrepresent that. The page exists so that anyone evaluating us on this requirement gets a straight answer today, before a trial rather than after one.

capabilities.title: What is intended
capabilities.body: A domestic content percentage per part or assembly, computed from material origin and processing location, with the calculation basis visible rather than hidden in a formula.

capabilities.title: Evidence behind the number
capabilities.body: The material records, certificates and processing evidence that support the percentage, attached to it, because the number is only as good as what backs it.

capabilities.title: Threshold checking
capabilities.body: Comparison against the applicable threshold for the contract, with a clear position rather than a figure you have to interpret alone.

capabilities.title: Enterprise scope
capabilities.body: If built, this would sit with ITAR, PPAP and USMCA as an Enterprise compliance module, matching how that group is tiered today.

capabilities.title: Why the evidence matters more than the number
capabilities.body: A percentage nobody can trace back to material records and processing evidence is a liability rather than an asset. Any implementation would have to attach the supporting records to the figure, not just store the figure.

howItWorks.name: Nothing works yet
howItWorks.text: There is no calculator and no domestic content data model in the product. This is a public statement of intent.

howItWorks.name: Thresholds and rules change
howItWorks.text: Domestic content thresholds have moved several times in recent years, so any implementation has to be configurable rather than hard-coded.

howItWorks.name: It builds on material tracking
howItWorks.text: Material tracking is live and would be the source, but it does not yet carry origin or processing-location attributes.

howItWorks.name: Status would change here first
howItWorks.text: If it moves into development it gets a milestone and a progress figure here, and a changelog entry on release.

howItWorks.name: What to do in the meantime
howItWorks.text: Keep the calculation wherever your contracts team keeps it today, and use live material tracking to hold the certificates and receipts that support it, so at least the evidence is on the order rather than in a folder.

items.name: On-premise deployment
items.metaDescription: Not generally available. On-premise or customer-cloud deployment is a Wave 3 Enterprise conversation with no committed date and no published price.
items.lead: This is not a product you can buy today. On-premise deployment is a Wave 3 Enterprise conversation, not a shipping option, and there is no committed date.
items.answer: On-premise deployment of KanchanFlow is not generally available. Our standard deployment is our USA data centres on AWS US-East and US-West. On-premise or customer-cloud deployment is a Wave 3 Enterprise conversation with no committed date and no published price, and it is listed as Contact Sales in our feature matrix for that reason.
summary: Some manufacturers cannot put customer data in a vendor's cloud — an ITAR obligation, a defence customer's requirement, or an internal policy that predates the argument. We would rather have that conversation honestly than pretend a self-hosted build exists. Most requirements described as on-premise turn out to be data residency or audit requirements, and those have a different and much shorter answer.

It does not. Today the product runs in our USA data centres, on AWS US-East and US-West, with no offshore replication. Enterprise customers with a genuine on-premise requirement should talk to us about what is possible and on what timescale, and the answer may be that we are not the right fit yet.

capabilities.title: What exists today
capabilities.body: USA data centres on AWS US-East and US-West, with no offshore replication, plus custom data residency as an Enterprise capability. That is the current answer to a data location requirement.

capabilities.title: What Contact Sales means
capabilities.body: A scoping conversation, not an order form. There is no published price, no packaged installer and no standard support model for an on-premise deployment.

capabilities.title: Why it is hard
capabilities.body: The AI agents, the WhatsApp Business API connection and the e-invoicing integrations all reach external services. An on-premise deployment has to answer what happens to each of those.

capabilities.title: Enterprise only
capabilities.body: If it becomes real, it is an Enterprise capability. Our feature matrix lists on-premise as Contact Sales under Enterprise and blank on the other tiers.

capabilities.title: What we would ask you first
capabilities.body: Which requirement is actually binding — where data is stored, who can audit it, or whether any external call is permitted at all. The three have very different answers, and only the third genuinely needs an on-premise build.

howItWorks.name: There is no installer
howItWorks.text: There is no packaged on-premise build. Anyone telling you a date for one at this stage would be guessing.

howItWorks.name: Start with the actual requirement
howItWorks.text: Most on-premise requirements are really data residency, data sovereignty or an audit requirement, and Enterprise custom data residency may already answer them.

howItWorks.name: Scope the external dependencies
howItWorks.text: AI agents, WhatsApp and e-invoicing all call out. Any deployment discussion has to establish which of those you can and cannot allow.

howItWorks.name: We may say no
howItWorks.text: If your requirement is a fully air-gapped install, we are not the right vendor today, and we will tell you that in the first call rather than the third.

faqs.a: A scoping conversation on an Enterprise account, not a purchasable option. There is no price, no installer and no committed date.

faqs.a: Often, yes. Most on-premise requirements are really about where data lives and who can audit it, and Enterprise custom data residency addresses both.

faqs.a: They call external services. Any on-premise conversation has to establish which external calls your policy permits, and sometimes the answer makes the deployment impossible.

items.name: Multi-company and multi-plant
items.metaDescription: Not built. Planned support for several legal entities and plants in one workspace with consolidated reporting. Wave 2, Q3 2027 direction, no committed date.
items.lead: This feature does not exist. Running several legal entities and plants in one workspace with a consolidated view is Wave 2 direction, indicatively Q3 2027, with no committed date.
items.answer: Multi-company and multi-plant support is not built. The intent is one KanchanFlow workspace holding several legal entities and plants, each invoicing correctly, with consolidated reporting across them. It is Wave 2 with a Q3 2027 direction and no committed date. Several Enterprise features in our matrix reference it, and none of them are available yet either.
summary: A manufacturer with two legal entities and three plants currently has an ugly choice: one workspace that cannot invoice correctly per entity, or separate workspaces with no consolidated view of a customer who buys from both. Neither is good, and we do not have a third answer today. Saying so on a public page is better than letting it surface in month two.

The intent is entities as first-class objects with their own tax registration, numbering and bank details, plants underneath them, and customer, pipeline and receivable roll-ups across the group. Our feature matrix already lists multi-entity as an Enterprise capability; that row describes the intended state, not a shipping one, and this page exists to say so.

capabilities.title: What is intended
capabilities.body: Legal entities with their own tax registration, document numbering, bank details and terms, with plants underneath, in one workspace.

capabilities.title: Consolidated customer view
capabilities.body: A customer group buying from two of your entities seen as one relationship with combined exposure — the Enterprise roll-up that customer 360 references.

capabilities.title: Correct documents per entity
capabilities.body: An invoice belongs to one entity and must carry that entity's registration and numbering. Getting this wrong is a tax problem, not a cosmetic one.

capabilities.title: Cross-entity reporting
capabilities.body: Pipeline, order book and receivables reported per entity and consolidated, in one base reporting currency.

capabilities.title: What breaks without it today
capabilities.body: A second legal entity means a second workspace, which means no shared customer view, no consolidated pipeline and duplicate account records. That is the honest cost of the current design, and it is why this is on the Wave 2 list.

howItWorks.name: Nothing works yet
howItWorks.text: One workspace is one operating entity today. Multi-entity is not implemented in any partial form.

howItWorks.name: It is a data model change
howItWorks.text: Entity has to sit above almost every record, which is why it is a Wave 2 item rather than something we can slot in.

howItWorks.name: Several features depend on it
howItWorks.text: Enterprise multi-entity roll-up in customer 360, multi-plant milestones on orders and multi-entity territory all wait on this.

howItWorks.name: Status would change here first
howItWorks.text: If it enters development this page gets a milestone and a progress figure, and the changelog gets an entry on release.

howItWorks.name: What to do in the meantime
howItWorks.text: Run one workspace per operating entity and accept the duplicate customer records, or run the group from one entity and invoice the second outside the system. Neither is good and we are not going to describe them as workarounds.

items.name: SSO
items.h1: SSO — SAML, Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace
items.metaDescription: Not built. Planned SAML single sign-on with Okta, Azure AD and Google Workspace for Enterprise. Wave 2, Q2 2027 direction, no committed date.
secondaryKeywords: azure ad single sign on software
items.lead: This feature does not exist. SAML single sign-on with Okta, Azure AD and Google Workspace is Wave 2 direction, indicatively Q2 2027, with no committed date.
items.answer: Single sign-on via SAML with Okta, Azure AD and Google Workspace is not built in KanchanFlow. Authentication today is email and password with multi-factor authentication available. SSO is a Wave 2 item with a Q2 2027 direction and no committed date; our feature matrix lists it under Enterprise as the intended state.
summary: For a shop of thirty people, email and password with multi-factor authentication is a reasonable answer. For a manufacturer with an IT policy, a joiners-movers-leavers process and an identity provider, it is a procurement objection — and often a legitimate one, because an account that survives someone's departure is a real risk.

SSO is on the Wave 2 list for that reason, targeted at SAML with Okta, Azure AD and Google Workspace. It is not built. If SSO is a hard requirement for you today, we would rather you knew that before a trial than after one. An objection found late in an evaluation wastes your time and ours.

capabilities.title: What is intended
capabilities.body: SAML 2.0 single sign-on with Okta, Azure AD and Google Workspace as the named providers, so access follows your identity provider rather than a separate password.

capabilities.title: Deprovisioning that actually works
capabilities.body: The real value is that removing someone in your identity provider removes their access here. That is the risk email-and-password leaves open.

capabilities.title: What exists today
capabilities.body: Email and password with multi-factor authentication, role-based permissions, and custom role-based access control on Enterprise.

capabilities.title: Enterprise scope
capabilities.body: The feature matrix lists SSO under Enterprise. That row describes the intended capability, not a shipping one.

capabilities.title: Why we are explicit about this
capabilities.body: SSO appears on Enterprise feature matrices across this category, and buyers reasonably assume a row means a shipping capability. Ours describes intent, so we mark it planned here rather than letting a trial discover it.

capabilities.title: What SSO would and would not change
capabilities.body: It would change how people sign in and how access is removed when they leave. It would not change role-based permissions, which already exist, or the audit log, which is a separate Professional and Enterprise capability being built for Wave 1 Milestone 5.

howItWorks.name: Nothing works yet
howItWorks.text: There is no SAML implementation and no identity provider integration in the product today.

howItWorks.name: Use MFA meanwhile
howItWorks.text: Multi-factor authentication is available now and is the practical control until SSO exists.

howItWorks.name: Deprovisioning is manual
howItWorks.text: Removing a leaver's access is an administrator action in the workspace today. It should be part of your offboarding checklist.

howItWorks.name: Status would change here first
howItWorks.text: Entering development would put a milestone and a progress figure on this page, with a changelog entry on release.

howItWorks.name: What to do in the meantime
howItWorks.text: Turn on multi-factor authentication for every user, use role-based permissions to limit what each account can reach, and put workspace deprovisioning explicitly on your offboarding checklist rather than assuming it happens.

tierAvailability.professional: Not available.
tierAvailability.enterprise: Planned for Enterprise. Not built, no committed date.

faqs.q: Is SSO available on Enterprise?
faqs.a: No. The feature matrix lists SSO under Enterprise as the intended capability. It is not built, and no tier has it today.

faqs.q: What authentication do you have now?
faqs.a: Email and password with multi-factor authentication, role-based permissions, and custom role-based access control on Enterprise.

faqs.q: When would SSO ship?
faqs.a: No committed date. Wave 2 with a Q2 2027 direction. If it firms up, this page changes and the changelog records the release.

faqs.q: How do I remove a leaver's access today?
faqs.a: An administrator removes the user in the workspace. Until SSO exists that step has to be on your offboarding checklist rather than automatic.

faqs.q: Which providers would you support?
faqs.a: SAML 2.0 with Okta, Azure AD and Google Workspace named first, because those are what our Enterprise conversations actually ask for. Other SAML-compliant providers would follow from the same implementation rather than needing separate work, but we are not going to list providers we have not tested.

items.name: Tally & TallyPrime
items.tagline: Push accepted quotes into TallyPrime as sales orders and pull payment status back, without anyone re-keying a voucher.
items.metaDescription: Tally integration for manufacturing CRM: push accepted quotes to TallyPrime as sales orders, sync GSTIN, HSN and payment status. Setup, limits, fixes.
items.answer: KanchanFlow, the RFQ-to-Order CRM, connects to Tally and TallyPrime over the local ODBC and XML gateway so an accepted quote becomes a Tally sales order with its GSTIN, HSN and line-level tax intact. Payment and outstanding balance flow back every fifteen minutes, so estimators can see who has paid before they quote again.
intro: Most shops we talk to keep Tally on one machine in the accounts room and the quoting process everywhere else. The result is a re-keying step: an estimator wins a job, prints the quote, walks it over, and someone types the same twelve line items into a Tally sales order two days later. That gap is where wrong HSN codes and stale customer masters come from.

This connector closes that gap in one direction and opens a window in the other. KanchanFlow writes the accepted quote into Tally as a sales order voucher, matched to the existing ledger by GSTIN rather than by name. Tally sends back the invoice number, the payment received against it, and the outstanding balance, so the CRM record shows what the accounts room already knows.
items.frame: This connector is for USA manufacturers with India operations, India-based contract customers, or manufacturers exporting to India. Tally is the books of record for the India entity; KanchanFlow is the quoting layer that feeds it.

syncTo.detail: Accepted quote becomes a Sales Order voucher with the quote number in the Reference field and the KanchanFlow quote ID in a UDF, so the two records stay traceable in both systems.
New customers are created under Sundry Debtors with GSTIN, state code, PAN and the registered billing address. Existing ledgers are matched on GSTIN first, PAN second, and never on name alone.
Each quote line maps to a Tally stock item by part number. If the item does not exist we create it with the HSN/SAC code, unit of measure and GST rate from the quote line.
CGST/SGST for intra-state and IGST for inter-state are computed from the place-of-supply state code on the quote, not copied from a default, so a Maharashtra-to-Gujarat order books as IGST.
The territory on the quote maps to a Tally cost centre, so revenue lands in the right regional bucket without an accountant re-tagging it at month end.
Quote revision number, estimator name and the RFQ source are written into the voucher narration for anyone auditing where a number came from.

syncFrom.detail: When accounts converts the sales order to an invoice, the invoice number and date appear on the KanchanFlow order record within one sync cycle.
Receipt vouchers allocated against the invoice reduce the outstanding amount shown on the customer 360 and on the order timeline.
Total outstanding and the 0-30 / 31-60 / 61-90 / 90+ ageing bucket per ledger, so an estimator can see a customer is 74 days overdue before quoting them again.
The credit limit set on the Tally ledger is read into the CRM and shown as a warning band on new quotes for that account.
Read once per day for the customer 360 header. This is a display value, not an accounting source of truth.

items.cadence: Every 15 minutes, or on demand from the record via Sync now

setup: In TallyPrime, open the company you want to connect and go to F11 Features and set Use ODBC to Yes. Note the ODBC port, which defaults to 9000.
Still in TallyPrime, enable the XML/HTTP gateway under Configure, Advanced Configuration, and set the Tally interface to act as both Client and Server.
Confirm Tally is reachable from the machine that will run the bridge by opening http://localhost:9000 in a browser. You should see a short XML response, not a blank page.
Download the KanchanFlow Tally Bridge from Settings, Integrations, Tally. It is a small Windows service, roughly 18 MB, that runs on the same machine or the same LAN as Tally.
Install the bridge as a Windows service, not as a foreground application. If it runs as a logged-in user, it stops syncing when that user logs off.
Paste the workspace pairing token from Settings, Integrations, Tally into the bridge configuration and click Pair. The token expires after 30 minutes.
Select the Tally company to bind. One KanchanFlow workspace binds to exactly one Tally company. If you keep multiple companies, run one bridge instance per company on separate ports.
Map your Tally voucher types. By default we write to Sales Order, but shops that use a custom voucher type must select it here before the first push.
Map units of measure. KanchanFlow ships EA, PC, KG, MTR, SET and LOT. Any unit you use in Tally that is not in that list must be mapped or the push will fail on that line.
Run the pre-flight check. It writes a test sales order for 1 unit into Tally, reads it back, and then cancels it. Do this outside working hours the first time.
Turn on Payment write-back if you want ageing and outstanding balances in the CRM. This is read-only against Tally and can be left off.
Push one real accepted quote and open it in Tally before you enable the connector for the whole team.
limitations: TallyPrime 3.0 or later, or Tally.ERP 9 release 6.6.3 or later. Older releases do not expose the sales-order fields we write and will fail the pre-flight check.
Tally has no cloud API. The bridge must run on a machine that is on the same network as Tally and switched on. If that machine sleeps, the queue holds but nothing syncs until it wakes.
One workspace to one Tally company. Multi-company groups need one bridge per company and cannot roll up inside the CRM.
We do not write purchase vouchers, journal entries, stock journals, payroll or any inventory movement. Sales orders and customer masters only.
We do not push quote attachments, drawings or terms and conditions text into Tally. Those stay in KanchanFlow.

Payment write-back is a read of allocated receipts. Advances, on-account receipts and unallocated credits will not reduce the outstanding figure we display, so our number can read higher than what accounts believes is owed.

troubleshooting.error: Pre-flight fails with Could not reach Tally at port 9000
troubleshooting.cause: Tally is not running, ODBC is off, or Windows Firewall is blocking the port on the bridge machine.
troubleshooting.fix: Open Tally, check F11 for ODBC set to Yes, then add an inbound rule for TCP 9000 on the private profile. Test with http://localhost:9000 before retrying.

troubleshooting.error: Push rejected: Ledger does not exist
troubleshooting.cause: The customer has no GSTIN in KanchanFlow, so we could not match a Sundry Debtors ledger and were not permitted to create one because ledger creation is off.
troubleshooting.fix: Add the GSTIN to the customer record, or turn on Create missing ledgers in the connector settings and re-push. Verify the created ledger's state code afterwards.

troubleshooting.error: Push rejected: Unit of measure not found
troubleshooting.cause: A quote line uses a unit that has no mapping to a Tally simple unit, most often a custom unit like SQFT or COIL.
troubleshooting.fix: Create the unit in Tally under Inventory Info, Units of Measure, then add the mapping in the connector's unit table and re-push the quote.

troubleshooting.error: Duplicate sales orders appear in Tally
troubleshooting.cause: Someone re-pushed a quote after the voucher was manually renumbered in Tally, so our reference lookup no longer matched.
troubleshooting.fix: Delete the duplicate voucher in Tally, then use Relink in the connector panel to bind the quote to the surviving voucher number. Do not renumber vouchers we have written.

troubleshooting.error: Tax computes as CGST/SGST on an inter-state order
troubleshooting.cause: The place-of-supply state code on the quote is blank or matches the company state, usually because the shipping address was typed as free text.
troubleshooting.fix: Set the state on the ship-to address in KanchanFlow, cancel the voucher in Tally, and re-push. The state code drives the tax split, not the address text.

faqs.q: Does this work with Tally on a cloud VPS?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as the bridge runs on that same VPS or on a machine with a private network route to it. We do not expose Tally to the public internet and we will not ask you to.

faqs.q: Will it change anything in Tally that I did not approve?
faqs.a: It writes sales order vouchers, and it creates ledgers and stock items only if you turn those two switches on. It never edits an existing voucher, never deletes anything, and never touches an invoice once accounts has raised it.

faqs.q: Which tiers include Tally?
faqs.a: Starter includes one accounting connector of your choice, so you can pick Tally. Professional and Enterprise include all three of Tally, Zoho Books and QuickBooks. A Starter shop that needs a second connector can add one for $15 per month.

faqs.q: What happens if Tally is closed when a quote is accepted?
faqs.a: The push queues. When the bridge next sees Tally running it drains the queue in order. The CRM record shows Queued rather than Synced so nobody assumes it landed.

faqs.q: Does it handle e-Invoice IRN generation?
faqs.a: No, that is the ClearTax GSP connector's job. Tally holds the voucher, ClearTax registers the IRN. The two connectors are independent and most India-facing shops run both.

faqs.q: Is my Tally data sent to your servers?
faqs.a: The bridge sends only the fields listed in the two sync tables on this page, over TLS, to your workspace. We do not copy your Tally company file, your ledger tree or any voucher we did not write.

items.tiers: All tiers — Starter selects one accounting connector; Professional and Enterprise include all three

items.name: Zoho Books
items.tagline: Turn an accepted quote into a Zoho Books sales order or invoice, and read payment status back onto the customer record.
items.metaDescription: Zoho Books integration for manufacturing CRM: post accepted quotes as sales orders or invoices and sync contacts, items and payment status. Setup and limits.
items.primaryKeyword: zoho books integration for manufacturing CRM
items.answer: KanchanFlow, the RFQ-to-Order CRM, connects to Zoho Books through the official OAuth API so an accepted quote posts as a sales order or invoice with its items, taxes and place of supply intact. Payments, credit notes and outstanding balances come back on a fifteen-minute cycle, which is the fastest write-back of the three accounting connectors we ship.
intro: Zoho Books is the easiest of our three accounting connectors to live with, because it is the only one with a real cloud API and no bridge software. You authorise once with OAuth, pick an organisation, and the connector runs server to server. Nothing has to stay switched on in your office for the sync to work.

What it does is narrow on purpose. KanchanFlow owns the RFQ, the cost buildup and the revision history. Zoho Books owns the ledger. The connector moves an accepted quote across that line as a sales order or an invoice, and brings back only what a salesperson needs to see: what was billed, what was paid, and what is overdue.
items.frame: This connector is for USA manufacturers with India operations, India-based contract customers, or manufacturers exporting to India. It also runs against the US, UK, EU, AU and global Zoho Books editions, but the GST fields described below only appear on the India edition.

syncTo.detail: You choose per workspace which one an accepted quote creates. Sales order is the default because it leaves accounts in control of when revenue is recognised.
Customer becomes a Zoho Books Contact matched on GSTIN, then on email domain. The quote's named buyer is written as a Contact Person so statements go to a human, not a generic inbox.
Each quote line posts with part number as item code, description, quantity, rate, HSN or SAC code and discount. Items missing from Zoho Books are created if item creation is enabled.

syncTo.field: Place of supply and tax treatment
syncTo.detail: Destination state drives the tax treatment field, so intra-state posts CGST plus SGST and inter-state posts IGST. Export orders post with the zero-rated treatment and the LUT reference if one is on file.
A text custom field carries the quote ID and revision number, which is what makes the record traceable back to the estimate that produced it.
The quote owner maps to a Zoho Books salesperson record so commission reporting in Books matches ownership in the CRM.

syncFrom.detail: Draft, sent, overdue, partially paid or paid, refreshed every cycle and shown as a badge on the order timeline.
Each payment against the invoice, with date, amount and mode, appears on the customer 360 payment strip.
Credit notes raised against a synced invoice appear on the order record so a salesperson does not chase money that has been credited back.
Read per contact and shown as a warning band on any new quote raised for that customer.
If accounts fixes a wrong GSTIN in Zoho Books, we pull the corrected value back rather than overwriting it on the next push.

items.cadence: Every 15 minutes, or on demand from the record via Sync now

setup: In KanchanFlow, open Settings, Integrations, Zoho Books and click Connect. You are sent to Zoho's own consent screen.
Sign in as a Zoho Books user with the Admin role. A Staff-role user can authorise the connection but cannot create the custom field in step six.
Review the requested scopes on the consent screen. We ask for contacts, items, sales orders, invoices, payments and credit notes, and nothing else. Approve.
Choose your Zoho Books organisation. If you run multiple organisations, one KanchanFlow workspace binds to one organisation.
Choose whether an accepted quote posts as a Sales Order or an Invoice. Sales Order is the safer default and is what we recommend for the first month.

Let the connector create its custom field. It adds one text field named KanchanFlow Quote ID to the sales order and invoice modules. Zoho Books allows a limited number of custom fields per module, so if you are at that ceiling you must free one first.
Map your tax rates. The connector reads your Books tax list and asks you to confirm which rate is your default GST rate and which is your zero-rated export rate.
