testing.note: Every connector on this page is re-tested end to end against a live sandbox each quarter, and the date of that test is printed on the page. If a date looks stale, the page is wrong and we want to hear about it.

cadence.headline: Two posts a week for weeks 1 to 10, then one a week
cadence.detail: The first twenty posts are the launch order below. Weeks 1 through 10 ship two posts a week; from week 11 the cadence drops to one a week so that each post can carry original working detail rather than a rewritten summary of the last one.

faqs.q: What is a good RFQ response time for a job shop?
faqs.a: Under 24 hours on a median basis is a defensible target for a shop doing mixed one-off work, and under four hours on repeat parts quoted from history. Complex new parts with outside operations should still take a day or more, and compressing those is a pricing risk rather than a productivity gain.

faqs.q: How do we measure it if RFQs arrive on four different channels?
faqs.a: Run the clock from the moment the request enters the business on any channel, not from when it enters your quoting system. Otherwise the number improves the day you buy software without a single hour of real delay having gone anywhere.

faqs.q: Which of the five fixes pays back fastest?
faqs.a: Routing. It is the largest block of time, it is queue time rather than work, and a shop can implement it with rules on a whiteboard before buying anything. Same-day no-bid discipline is second and also costs nothing.

faqs.q: Does faster response mean worse quotes?
faqs.a: Only if you compress the estimating on complex parts, which is why we separate the segments. The median falls because easy quotes stop waiting in a queue. The hard quotes take exactly as long as they always did, and they should.

faqs.q: Our estimators say they are already at capacity. Does this help or hurt?
faqs.a: It helps, because most of the recovered time is not estimating time. Routing removes queue time, and same-day no-bids remove work that was never going to convert. A shop that clears its no-bids and incomplete requests daily typically recovers about a day a week of estimating capacity.

faqs.q: Should we tell customers our response time target?
faqs.a: Once you can hold it, yes. A stated target that you meet is a differentiator with purchasing agents, who track supplier responsiveness informally whether or not they have a formal scorecard. A stated target you miss is worse than saying nothing.

faqs.q: What if the delay is the customer, not us?
faqs.a: That is common and worth measuring separately. Park incomplete RFQs with a clock on the outstanding question, and report time waiting on the customer as its own segment. It stops your internal number being distorted, and it gives you something concrete to raise with a buyer who habitually sends incomplete packages.

posts.title: How to cut RFQ response time from three days to three hours
posts.metaTitle: Cut RFQ response time from days to hours
posts.description: Where the three days actually go in a job shop, measured stage by stage, and the five changes that recover them in the order they pay back.
posts.answer: RFQ response time is the elapsed hours from a request for quote arriving to a priced quote leaving. In most job shops it runs three to five days, and most of that is queue time before an estimator opens the file. KanchanFlow is an RFQ-to-Order CRM that runs that clock from arrival.

sections.h2: The number almost nobody measures
paragraphs: Ask a shop owner how long it takes to turn an RFQ around and you will usually get a number between one and two days. Ask them to prove it and the conversation changes, because the arrival time of an RFQ is a timestamp in somebody's mail client and the send time is a timestamp in a different one, and nobody has ever subtracted the two across a month of requests.

When shops do measure it properly, the number is nearly always worse than the estimate. Three to five days is the common range for a shop running two estimators on forty inbound requests a week. That gap between what a shop believes and what it does is not dishonesty. It is that the memorable RFQs are the ones handled fast, and the ones that sat for four days are memorable to nobody except the buyer who stopped waiting.

The reason to care is not tidiness. A purchasing agent placing a one-off part is solving a problem this week. They will typically send the same package to three or four shops and place the order with the first credible quote back, adjusting only if the price is out of line. Response time is not a service metric in that situation. It is the qualifying round.

sections.h2: Break the clock into three segments
paragraphs: A single response-time number is not actionable, because it hides three very different problems inside one figure. Split it into intake-to-assignment, assignment-to-priced, and priced-to-sent, and the answer is usually obvious within a week of data.

Intake-to-assignment is the time between the RFQ arriving anywhere in your business and it having a named owner. Assignment-to-priced is real estimating work. Priced-to-sent is approval, document assembly and the actual send.

In the shops we have looked at, the split is lopsided in a consistent direction. Intake-to-assignment is frequently the largest of the three and it is almost entirely queue time — the RFQ existing, unread, in a shared inbox. Assignment-to-priced is the segment everyone assumes is the problem and it is usually the smallest lever. Priced-to-sent is small in absolute terms but has a nasty tail when a margin exception needs an owner who is on the floor.
list: Intake to assignment: often 40 to 60 percent of the total, almost all of it queue time
Assignment to priced: the real estimating work, and the segment hardest to compress safely
Priced to sent: usually short, with a long tail whenever an approval is needed

sections.h2: Fix one: give every RFQ an owner within minutes, not mornings
paragraphs: The single largest recoverable block of time is the period where an RFQ has arrived and nobody has decided who is dealing with it. In most shops that decision happens at a morning huddle, which means an RFQ arriving at 10:15 on Tuesday waits until Wednesday to be assigned even though nobody was busy.

Routing rules replace the huddle for the ordinary cases. Sort on material, process, part envelope and named customer: stainless weldments to the fabrication estimator, five-axis work to the machinist who quotes five-axis, anything past your table travel flagged before an estimator spends an hour on a job you cannot hold.

The exception cases still need a person, and that is fine. The point is that the ninety percent of requests with an obvious owner get one immediately, and the huddle is spent on the ten percent that genuinely need discussion. Shops that make this one change typically remove a day from the median before touching anything else.

sections.h2: Fix two: stop retyping the request
paragraphs: The second block of lost time is transcription. An RFQ arrives as an email with a PDF drawing and a spreadsheet of quantities. Somebody opens the spreadsheet, retypes the part numbers into a quoting sheet, and copies the quantities across. On a forty-line request that is twenty minutes of work that produces no value and introduces at least one error.

Extraction from the attachment removes most of it. The important design decision is that extraction produces a draft an estimator confirms, never a record the software commits on its own. On a clean tabular bill of material the extraction is usually complete. On a scanned print with handwritten annotations it will get the part number and miss the callout, and it should say so rather than guessing.

The measurable effect is smaller than the routing fix but it compounds, because it applies to every RFQ rather than to the ones that were queued. It also removes a specific and expensive error class: a quantity transposed at transcription and never noticed until the purchase order arrives at a different number.

sections.h2: Fix three: quote from your own history, not from a blank sheet
paragraphs: The assignment-to-priced segment is the one shops most want to attack and the one where naive speed-ups do damage. You cannot make an estimator think faster, and a quote produced in half the time by skipping the outside-service check is not a better quote.

What does work is starting from a reference. When a print arrives for a 4140 shaft, two inches in diameter, fourteen inches long, with a keyway and a ground journal, the estimator should see the last three comparable parts you quoted, what each was quoted at, what was accepted, and what the material and setup actually were. That is not an automatic price. It is the difference between an empty grid and a defensible starting point.

In practice this takes a ninety-minute estimate down to something closer to twenty-five, and the quality goes up rather than down, because the estimator is comparing against a real prior job rather than reconstructing an approach from memory at the end of a long day.

sections.h2: Fix four: make approvals reachable from the shop floor
paragraphs: The priced-to-sent segment has a short median and a long tail. Most quotes need no approval and go straight out. The ones that breach a margin floor or a value threshold wait for the owner, and the owner is usually on the floor, at a customer, or under a machine.

A quote sitting on a desk waiting for a signature is the most annoying form of delay because the work is already done. Push the approval to a phone with the quote, the breached rule and the estimator's written reason attached, and the decision happens in the aisle between two setups. Fifteen seconds instead of a day and a half.

There is a discipline point attached. An approval rule that fires on most quotes will be ignored within a fortnight, and an ignored rule is worse than no rule. Four rules cover the exceptions worth catching: margin below the floor for that part family, total above a value threshold, a new customer with no credit history, and a lead time beyond what you can hold.

sections.h2: Fix five: decline faster
paragraphs: The uncomfortable arithmetic is that a two-estimator shop receiving forty requests a week cannot price forty requests properly. Something between eighteen and twenty-two of them will not get a real quote. The only question is whether that is a decision or an accident.

Made deliberately, a same-day no-bid costs five minutes and buys back an afternoon. It also does something counterintuitive: it protects the relationship. A purchasing agent with a part to place is running their own clock, and a fast, honest decline lets them move on. A week of silence costs them a week and teaches them not to send you the next one.

Record the reason every time. Outside our envelope, lead time we cannot hold, price target below our floor, a customer we no longer serve. After a quarter the no-bid report is the cheapest market research a shop has, and it usually shows a pattern worth acting on — one buyer sending work you never win, or a process you keep declining that might be worth buying capacity for.
list: Outside our machining envelope or capability
Lead time inside our current backlog for that machine group
Target price below our margin floor for that part family
Incomplete package, and the buyer did not answer the technical question
Customer on credit hold or outside the terms we accept

sections.h2: What three hours actually looks like
paragraphs: Three hours is not a target for every request and it is not achieved by working faster. It is achieved by sorting the requests into the ones that can be answered from history and the ones that need real work, and answering the first group immediately.

A repeat part from a known customer, quoted from the last accepted revision with a check on current material cost, is a twenty-minute job that should leave the same morning. A similar part with a reference buildup to adjust is under an hour. A genuinely new part in a difficult material with three outside operations is a day and should be, and pretending otherwise is how shops win work they lose money on.

The honest headline is that the median moves from days to hours while the hardest quotes take exactly as long as they always did. That is the right outcome. Compressing the estimating on a complex part is not a productivity gain, it is a pricing risk.

sections.h2: Measure it weekly and split it by channel
paragraphs: Once the clock is running from arrival rather than from when somebody noticed, look at the median weekly and split it two ways: by estimator and by intake channel.

The estimator split is a coaching tool, not a scoreboard, and it should be handled that way or people will start gaming the timestamps. The channel split is more immediately useful. Shops routinely find that email RFQs are answered in a day and web form submissions sit for four, because the form sends a notification to an address nobody treats as urgent.

That kind of finding is worth more than any software feature, and you cannot see it without measuring from arrival. It is also the reason to run the clock from the moment a request enters the business rather than from the moment it enters your quoting system — otherwise the number improves the day you buy software and none of the delay has actually gone anywhere.

sections.h2: The order to do this in
paragraphs: Routing first, because it is the largest block and the cheapest to change. Same-day no-bid discipline second, because it recovers estimating capacity immediately and costs nothing. History-based quoting third, because it needs some data behind it before it pays. Extraction fourth. Mobile approvals last, because the tail they fix is real but narrow.

None of this requires buying anything to start. A shop with a shared inbox and a whiteboard can implement routing rules and a same-day no-bid policy on Monday. What software adds is that the clock runs by itself, the rules apply without anybody remembering them, and the history is reachable from the quoting screen instead of living in a folder of PDFs.
If you take one thing from this: measure from arrival, not from assignment. Every improvement described here is invisible unless the clock starts when the buyer pressed send.

faqs.q: Does Section 43B(h) apply to a US company with no Indian entity?
faqs.a: No. It applies to a taxpayer claiming a deduction on an Indian income tax return. If you import parts from India into the United States and have no Indian entity, this provision does not reach you. It applies where a US manufacturer has an India entity buying from Indian suppliers.

faqs.q: Is the deduction lost or just delayed?
faqs.a: Delayed. The expense moves to the financial year in which it is actually paid rather than the year it accrued. The cost is the timing shift and its cash consequence, not the loss of the expense.

faqs.q: Does it apply to medium enterprises?
faqs.a: No. Only micro and small enterprises registered under the MSMED Act are in scope. Applying it to medium suppliers overstates your exposure and produces a report your finance team will stop trusting.

faqs.q: What is the fastest way to reduce exposure?
faqs.a: Put written supply agreements in place with your regular Indian suppliers specifying payment terms inside 45 days. Without a written agreement the statutory limit is 15 days, so this single change converts most of your spend from a 15-day clock to a 45-day one.

faqs.q: Does a payment term on our purchase order count as a written agreement?
faqs.a: That is exactly the kind of question to put to an Indian chartered accountant rather than to a software vendor. A term the supplier never signed is generally weaker than a signed supply agreement, and the safe course is a signed agreement.

faqs.q: Is the interest liability separate from the tax effect?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is often larger. Section 16 of the MSMED Act makes a late-paying buyer liable for compound interest at three times the RBI bank rate, compounded monthly. Most small suppliers do not invoice for it, which makes it a contingent liability rather than an absent one.

faqs.q: Is this tracking included in your Starter plan?
faqs.a: Yes. The MSMED 43B(h) tracker, GST invoicing, GSTIN validation, HSN classification and e-Invoice IRN are included on every tier including Starter. Gating a regulatory obligation behind an upgrade would be indefensible. Enterprise adds an aggregated multi-entity exposure calculator on top.

posts.title: Section 43B(h) explained for manufacturers buying from Indian MSMEs
posts.description: A US manufacturer's guide to India's MSME payment rule: what Section 43B(h) does, the 45-day and 15-day clocks, and who it actually applies to.
posts.answer: Section 43B(h) of India's Income Tax Act allows a deduction for payment to a registered micro or small enterprise only in the year it is paid, unless paid within the MSMED window — 45 days with a written agreement, 15 without. KanchanFlow, an RFQ-to-Order CRM, tracks that clock on every tier.

sections.h2: Why a US manufacturer should read this at all
paragraphs: If your business is entirely domestic, this does not apply to you and you can stop here. It applies where a US manufacturer has an India entity — an owned plant, a machining operation, an assembly or engineering office — that buys goods or services from Indian suppliers and files an Indian tax return.

A large share of Indian suppliers to manufacturers are registered as micro or small enterprises under the MSMED Act. Castings, forgings, machining subcontract, tooling, packaging, transport, and a great deal of professional services. If your India entity buys from them, the rule reaches your accounts.

It is worth being precise about what this is not. It is not a US obligation, it is not a customs or trade matter, and it does not apply because you import parts from India into the United States. It applies to an Indian taxpayer claiming a deduction on an Indian tax return.

sections.h2: What the provision actually does
paragraphs: Section 43B of India's Income Tax Act is a general rule that certain expenses are deductible only when actually paid, rather than when accrued. Clause (h), added by the Finance Act 2023 with effect from assessment year 2024-25, added payments to micro and small enterprises to that list — with an important carve-out.

The carve-out is that if the payment is made within the time limit specified in Section 15 of the MSMED Act, the normal accrual treatment applies. Pay inside the window and nothing changes. Pay outside it and the deduction moves to the year of actual payment.

So the mechanism is a timing shift, not a penalty and not a disallowance. An expense accrued in one financial year and paid late is deducted in the year it is paid instead. The cash cost of that shift depends on the rate and the gap, and on whether the payment crosses a year end at all.

sections.h2: The two clocks: 45 days and 15 days
paragraphs: Section 15 of the MSMED Act sets the payment window. Where there is a written agreement between buyer and supplier specifying a payment term, the limit is that term, capped at 45 days from the day of acceptance or deemed acceptance. Where there is no written agreement, the limit is 15 days.

That distinction catches manufacturers out more than anything else in the rule. A shop that buys castings on a handshake and pays at 30 days is outside the window, because with no written agreement the limit is 15. The same shop with a signed supply agreement specifying 45-day terms is inside it.

Acceptance is the other subtlety. The clock starts from the day of acceptance of the goods or services, or from the day of deemed acceptance where no objection is raised in writing within 15 days of delivery. For a manufacturer with an incoming inspection process that sometimes rejects a lot, the acceptance date and the delivery date are not the same day, and the difference matters.
list: Written agreement in place: the agreed term, capped at 45 days from acceptance
No written agreement: 15 days from acceptance
Acceptance means acceptance, or deemed acceptance if no written objection within 15 days of delivery
The clock is on the buyer, and the supplier's registration status is what triggers it

sections.h2: Who counts as a micro or small enterprise
paragraphs: The classification comes from investment in plant and machinery and from turnover, and the supplier must be registered — the Udyam registration is the practical evidence. Micro and small are the two categories in scope. Medium enterprises are not covered by this provision, which is a distinction people routinely get wrong.

The registration is also the thing you can actually check. A supplier either has a Udyam registration number with a micro or small classification or they do not, and it is verifiable. A supplier's own assertion in an email is not a substitute, and neither is a line on their letterhead from three years ago — classifications change as businesses grow.

There is also a trading exception worth knowing: the provision is generally understood to apply to suppliers of goods and services rather than to traders registered only as such. If a meaningful share of your spend is with intermediaries rather than manufacturers, that is a question for your Indian tax adviser rather than for a software vendor, and we are not going to pretend otherwise.

sections.h2: A worked example of the exposure
paragraphs: Take an India entity of a US manufacturer with an annual spend of around 6 crore rupees with subcontract machining and casting suppliers, of which roughly 40 percent is with registered micro and small enterprises. That is about 2.4 crore of in-scope spend.

Suppose the entity habitually pays at 60 days against no written agreement. Every one of those payments is outside the 15-day window. At any given year end, the open payable to in-scope suppliers might be around 40 lakh. That 40 lakh of expense is not deductible in the year it accrued; it moves to the following year.

The cost is not 40 lakh. It is the tax on 40 lakh, brought forward by one year, plus whatever the cash consequence of a larger current-year tax payment is for a business that is already funding working capital. It is a real number and it is entirely avoidable by paying inside the window or by putting written terms in place — and the second one costs nothing but a signature.

sections.h2: What this looks like as a process, not a year-end panic
paragraphs: The failure mode is always the same. Nobody knows which suppliers are registered micro or small, nobody knows which invoices are past the window, and the whole thing becomes a scramble in the fortnight before the return is filed, reconstructed from a payables ledger that does not carry the registration status.

Three things fix it, and none of them are complicated. Capture the Udyam registration and classification on the supplier record at onboarding, not at year end. Put written agreements in place with your regular suppliers specifying terms within 45 days, which converts a 15-day clock into a 45-day one across most of your spend. And run a report every month showing in-scope payables against their acceptance dates.
That third item is the one that changes behaviour, because it turns a tax provision into an operational number a finance person can act on while there is still time to pay.
list: Record Udyam registration and classification on the supplier at onboarding
Put written supply agreements in place with terms inside 45 days
Record the acceptance date, not just the invoice date
Report in-scope open payables monthly against the applicable clock
Review classification annually — suppliers move between categories as they grow

sections.h2: The interest liability nobody budgets for
paragraphs: Section 43B(h) is the tax consequence, and it gets the attention because it lands on a return. There is a second consequence that sits in the MSMED Act itself and is commercially larger for a manufacturer with a lot of small suppliers.

Section 16 of the MSMED Act makes a buyer who pays outside the window liable to pay compound interest to the supplier, at three times the Reserve Bank of India bank rate, compounded monthly, from the day after the window closed. That is not a rate anybody would agree to voluntarily, and it is not waived by a payment term in your own purchase order — a contractual term cannot override the statutory limit.

In practice most small suppliers do not invoice for it, because they would rather keep the business. That does not make the liability go away; it makes it a contingent item sitting quietly in your payables. It surfaces when a relationship ends badly, when a supplier is acquired, or during a due diligence exercise, which are exactly the three moments when a manufacturer least wants an unquantified historical liability.

There is also a disclosure dimension. Companies subject to Indian statutory audit are required to disclose amounts due to micro and small enterprises, including interest, in the notes to their accounts. A finance team that cannot identify in-scope suppliers cannot produce that disclosure accurately, which is a separate and quite visible problem.

sections.h2: Five mistakes manufacturers make with this rule
paragraphs: The first and most common is assuming a standard 30-day or 45-day payment term protects you. Without a written agreement the statutory limit is 15 days regardless of what your purchase order says, and a purchase order term the supplier never signed is generally not the written agreement contemplated here.

The second is treating medium enterprises as in scope. They are not. Applying the rule to every supplier with a Udyam registration overstates the exposure and produces a report nobody trusts, which is how a control quietly gets abandoned.

The third is running the clock from the invoice date. The statute runs it from acceptance or deemed acceptance, which for a manufacturer with incoming inspection can be days later — or, where a lot is rejected and replaced, considerably later. Recording an acceptance date is a small operational change with a direct effect on the numbers.

The fourth is checking registration once and never again. Classification depends on investment and turnover, and a growing supplier moves from micro to small to medium over a few years. An annual refresh of registration status across your active supplier base is enough. The fifth is leaving the whole exercise until the tax return, which converts a manageable monthly report into a fortnight of reconstruction with no time left to pay anybody.

sections.h2: Where a CRM fits, and where it does not
paragraphs: This is a payables and tax matter, and the definitive work belongs to your Indian accounting system and your tax adviser. We do not file returns, we do not compute a tax provision, and nothing in this article is tax advice.

What we hold is the commercial record around it: the supplier, their Udyam registration and classification, the purchase commitment, the acceptance date and the applicable clock on each payable. The MSMED 43B(h) tracker flags which suppliers are in scope and which payables are approaching or past the window, and it is included on every tier — Starter included — because gating a regulatory obligation behind an upgrade would be indefensible.

Enterprise adds an aggregated exposure calculator across entities, which matters if you run more than one Indian entity. The underlying tracker does not change between tiers, and neither does GST invoicing, GSTIN validation, HSN classification or e-Invoice IRN generation.

sections.h2: The short version
paragraphs: If your India entity buys from registered micro and small suppliers, pay them inside 45 days where you have written terms and inside 15 days where you do not, and the provision never touches you. If you pay late, the deduction moves to the year of payment, which is a cash timing cost rather than a lost expense.

The two changes with the best return are putting written agreements in place with your regular suppliers, which converts most of your spend from a 15-day clock to a 45-day one, and capturing registration status at supplier onboarding so the question can be answered in a report rather than reconstructed in March.

And take the actual advice from an Indian chartered accountant who can look at your specific facts. The provision has interpretive edges — trading suppliers, deemed acceptance, disputed invoices — where a general article is not a safe substitute for someone who is accountable for the answer.

faqs.q: What is the actual difference between an ERP and a CRM?
faqs.a: An ERP runs the inside of the business — materials, inventory, scheduling, job costing, what a job cost when it ran. A CRM runs the outside — who asked for what, what you quoted, which revision they hold, whether you followed up. The boundary is the customer. Work that happens before a purchase order exists is CRM work. Work that happens after it is ERP work.

faqs.q: Which one should a 30-person shop buy first?
faqs.a: Whichever side is losing you money faster, and that is usually knowable in an afternoon. If quotes go out late, RFQs get lost and nobody can say which revision a customer holds, the front office is the leak. If jobs run late, material arrives wrong and you cannot tell what a job actually cost, the floor is the leak. Shops that buy an ERP to fix a quoting problem end up with a slower quoting problem.

faqs.q: Can one system do both?
faqs.a: Several claim to, and the claim is usually true in the sense that both modules exist. What is worth checking is which half was the design centre. Production-first systems tend to have thin quoting and account history; sales-first systems tend to have no real production context. Neither is dishonest — it is just where the engineering went.

faqs.q: Does KanchanFlow integrate with our ERP?
faqs.a: There is no packaged connector for a named ERP — nothing you switch on for NetSuite or Epicor. Two narrower things do exist: production milestone updates can arrive over an ERP webhook on Professional and Enterprise, and an Enterprise workspace can commission a custom ERP connector for SAP, Oracle or similar as a paid add-on. What is packaged and live is accounting: QuickBooks Online and Enterprise, Zoho Books, Tally and MyOB, each with a published field-level sync table.

faqs.q: Is a spreadsheet ever the right answer?
faqs.a: For a shop doing five quotes a week with one estimator, often yes. The spreadsheet stops working at a fairly predictable point: when more than one person needs the same number at the same time, or when you cannot answer what you quoted six months ago. Until you hit one of those, buying software is solving a problem you do not have yet.

faqs.q: What does 'integrated' usually mean in practice?
faqs.a: Ask three questions. What fields move, in which direction, and how often? Is it a native connector, a middleware subscription, or a CSV export somebody runs on Fridays? And what happens when it fails — do you find out, or does a stale number sit on a screen looking current? A vendor who can answer all three in writing is describing an integration. One who cannot is describing an intention.

faqs.q: We already have an ERP we dislike. Should we replace it or add a CRM?
faqs.a: Separate the complaints first. If the complaint is that quoting is miserable, account history is unreachable and nobody chases quotes, adding a CRM is cheaper, faster and lower risk than an ERP migration. If the complaint is that scheduling is wrong and costing is untrustworthy, a CRM will not touch it. Most shops who say they hate their ERP are describing the front office half of it.

posts.title: ERP vs CRM for manufacturers: which one do you need first?
posts.metaTitle: ERP vs CRM for manufacturers: which comes first
posts.description: An ERP runs the shop. A CRM runs the customer side. Which a manufacturer needs first depends on where work is being lost — here is how to tell, with examples.
posts.answer: An ERP runs the inside of a manufacturing business: materials, scheduling, inventory and job costing. A CRM runs the customer side: RFQs, quotes, revisions and follow-up. KanchanFlow is an RFQ-to-Order CRM, not an ERP, and which one a shop should buy first depends on where work is being lost.

sections.h2: The one-line difference, and why it gets blurred
paragraphs: An ERP runs the inside of the business. A CRM runs the outside. The boundary between them is the purchase order: everything before it is a conversation with a customer, and everything after it is a job in your building.

That line is clean in theory and blurred in practice, because both categories have spent a decade selling into the other's territory. Every shop ERP now advertises a CRM module. Every CRM now advertises quoting. So a manufacturer comparing four products finds all four claiming to do the same nine things, and the comparison collapses into a feature checklist that tells them nothing.
The question that does not collapse is which half the product was designed around. That is usually visible in the first ten minutes of a demo, and it is almost never in the feature list.

sections.h2: What an ERP actually does in a manufacturing business
paragraphs: An ERP or MRP system exists to answer questions about work and materials. What do we need to buy, and when. Which machine runs this job on Thursday. How many bars are on the rack. What did this job cost when it actually ran, as opposed to what we said it would cost when we quoted it.

Those questions share a property: they are all about capacity and consumption inside your four walls. They need a bill of materials, a routing, a calendar and an inventory position. That is a large and specific set of machinery, and it is why ERP implementations are long.
list: Bill of materials and multi-level explosion
Purchasing, receiving and inventory position
Routings, capacity and production scheduling
Shop-floor data collection and job costing
What a job cost when it ran, against what it was quoted at

sections.h2: What a CRM actually does in a manufacturing business
paragraphs: A CRM exists to answer questions about customers and commitments. Who asked us for what. What did we quote, against which drawing revision. Did anyone follow up. What did this customer accept last time, and are we still pricing off a material cost from before the last move.

In a manufacturing business those questions have a shape that generalist CRMs do not carry. The unit of work is a request for quote with several parts on it, not a lead. There is no product catalogue, because the line item is the output of an estimate. And the same quote exists at Rev 0, Rev A and Rev B at three different prices, which a system built around one amount per opportunity has nowhere to put.
list: RFQ intake from every channel requests actually arrive on
Cost buildup and the estimate behind each line
Every revision of every quote, kept permanently
Follow-up cadence, and who owns which account
Purchase order matching against the revision that was accepted

sections.h2: Where they overlap, and where the overlap causes trouble
paragraphs: Three areas genuinely sit on the boundary: quoting, the customer record, and the order. Both categories have a claim on all three, and this is where most buying mistakes happen.

Quoting is the sharpest case. A shop ERP can produce a quote, because it has the cost data. What it usually cannot do is hold six variants of the same part, keep a revision chain that is never trimmed, or tell you what the customer opened and when. A CRM can do all of those and usually cannot see what the job actually cost when it ran. Both halves of that sentence are true at the same time, which is why so many shops end up quoting in a spreadsheet sitting next to an ERP that theoretically quotes.

The order is the second case, and it is where the wrong revision reaches the floor. A quote is accepted at Rev B, the purchase order arrives quoting a price from Rev A, and somebody has to notice. That reconciliation is CRM work, and the handoff afterwards is ERP work, and the gap between them is where the expensive errors live.

sections.h2: How to tell which one you need first
paragraphs: This is answerable without a consultant. Spend one afternoon writing down where work stopped moving in the last month, and sort what you find into two columns.

If most of what you wrote is in the first column, the front office is your constraint and a CRM is the cheaper, faster, lower-risk purchase. If most of it is in the second, an ERP or MRP is the answer and a CRM will not touch the problem. If it is genuinely split, fix the front office first — it is a shorter implementation and it produces the demand data that makes the ERP decision better.
list: Front office: RFQs sitting unread, quotes going out days late, nobody following up, arguments about which revision was quoted, repeat parts still priced off a stale material cost
Floor: jobs late, material arriving wrong or late, machines idle while work waits, no reliable answer to what a job cost, inventory counts that nobody trusts

sections.h2: The case for buying neither yet
paragraphs: A fifteen-person shop doing five quotes a week with one estimator often does not have a software problem. It has a template problem and a follow-up problem, and both are fixable in an afternoon for nothing.

Standardise the quote document so every quote carries the same fields, including the drawing revision it was priced against and an explicit validity date. Put the outstanding quotes on a single list with the date each was sent, and look at it every Monday. Write down your machine-group rates and your margin floor and stop rederiving them per quote.

If those three changes fix it, you have saved a subscription and a month of implementation. If after two months the list is still the problem — because more than one person needs it, or because nobody keeps it current — then the constraint is real and buying something is justified. That is a much better position to buy from than buying to find out.

sections.h2: What 'integrated' means, and what it usually means
paragraphs: Every vendor on both sides of this comparison will tell you they integrate with the other. The word covers an enormous range, and the difference between the ends of that range is months of work.

Three questions separate them, and any honest vendor can answer all three in writing. Which specific fields move, in which direction? Is it a native connector, a paid middleware subscription, or a CSV somebody exports on Friday afternoons? And when it breaks, do you get told, or does a stale number sit on a screen looking current until somebody quotes off it?

We should be held to the same standard, so, precisely: we ship no packaged connector for a named ERP. Production milestones can arrive over an ERP webhook on Professional and Enterprise, and an Enterprise workspace can commission a custom ERP connector for SAP, Oracle or similar as a paid add-on — bespoke work, not a switch. What is packaged and live is accounting: QuickBooks Online and Enterprise, Zoho Books, Tally and MyOB, each with a field-level table on its own page showing exactly what moves in each direction and what does not.

sections.h2: Why we are a CRM and not an ERP
paragraphs: KanchanFlow is not an ERP, MRP, CAD, BOM or advanced CPQ system. That sentence appears in our own build contract, and it is a scope commitment rather than a disclaimer.

The reason is that the two problems want different products. Doing production scheduling well requires a model of capacity and material that takes years to get right, and every company that has tried to bolt it onto a CRM has produced something thin. The same is true in reverse, which is why the CRM module inside most shop ERPs is the part nobody opens.

So we run the customer side end to end — intake, estimate, quote, revisions, acceptance, purchase order matching, order handoff — and we stop at the point where your ERP should take over. If you do not have an ERP, plenty of shops our size run on an accounting system and a whiteboard, and that is a legitimate arrangement for longer than most vendors will admit.

faqs.q: What does RFQ stand for?
faqs.a: Request for quotation. In manufacturing it is a buyer's formal request for a firm price and lead time against a defined specification — normally a drawing at a stated revision, with a quantity, a material callout and a required date.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an RFQ and a purchase order?
faqs.a: An RFQ asks for a price; a purchase order places the work. The RFQ comes first and creates no obligation on either side. The purchase order should be matched line for line against the quote revision the buyer accepted before anything is cut.

faqs.q: Is an RFQ legally binding?
faqs.a: The request itself is not. The quote you send in response usually is, for the validity period stated on it, which is why a validity window and a clear list of inclusions and exclusions belong on every quote. Take the definitive answer on your own terms from your attorney.

faqs.q: How many fields does a complete RFQ need?
faqs.a: Nine, in practice: part number and revision, drawing, quantity and breaks, material specification, process and outside operations, inspection requirements, required date, packaging and shipping, and the buyer's terms. Roughly a third of inbound RFQs arrive complete.

faqs.q: Should we quote every RFQ we receive?
faqs.a: No shop with more requests than estimating hours can, so the real choice is whether the filtering is deliberate. Triage on part family, quantity band, customer history and whether the work sits inside your capability envelope, and decline the rest the same day with a recorded reason.

faqs.q: Why does the drawing revision matter so much?
faqs.a: Because a quote priced against revision C and a purchase order placed against revision D are different jobs, and the difference is normally discovered after material has been cut. Recording which revision a quote priced, and matching the PO against it, is the only reliable protection.

faqs.q: What is an RFQ number for?
faqs.a: It is the thread that ties the request to the quote, the revisions, the acceptance, the purchase order and the order handed to production. Without it, each of those documents is a separate island and the connection lives in somebody's memory.

terms.title: What is an RFQ in manufacturing?
terms.description: An RFQ is a buyer's formal request for a price against a defined specification — part, drawing revision, quantity, material and date. How to handle one.
terms.answer: An RFQ, or request for quotation, is a buyer's formal request for a price against a defined specification. In manufacturing it carries a part number, a drawing revision, a quantity and a material callout, and expects a firm price and lead time. KanchanFlow is an RFQ-to-Order CRM built around that record.

sections.h2: The short definition
paragraphs: A request for quotation is the document a buyer sends when they know what they want and need to know what it costs. The defining characteristic is that the specification is settled. The buyer is not exploring options or asking how you would approach a problem; they are asking for a firm number against a drawing.
That distinction is what separates an RFQ from the two documents it is most often confused with, and it decides how a manufacturer should respond to each.

sections.h2: RFQ vs RFP vs RFI: what each one asks for
paragraphs: A request for information, or RFI, comes earlier. The buyer is mapping the market: who can do this kind of work, what capacity do they have, what certifications do they hold, what are their typical lead times. There is often no drawing attached and no firm quantity. The correct response is a capability statement, not a price, and a shop that answers an RFI with a detailed quote has spent estimating hours on a document that was never going to produce an order.

A request for proposal, or RFP, sits at the other end. The buyer has a problem rather than a specification, and they are asking suppliers to propose a solution. RFPs are common in engineer-to-order work, capital equipment and systems integration. The response is a proposal with a scope, a technical approach, assumptions, exclusions and a commercial structure. It takes days or weeks rather than hours.

An RFQ is the middle case and the most common one in job shop and contract manufacturing work. The specification exists, usually as a drawing at a stated revision. The buyer wants a price, a lead time and a validity period. What they are comparing across suppliers is largely price and delivery, which is why response time matters disproportionately.

sections.h2: What a complete RFQ contains
paragraphs: A well-formed manufacturing RFQ carries enough information that an estimator can price it without asking a question. In practice perhaps a third of inbound RFQs meet that standard, and chasing the missing information is one of the largest single consumers of estimating time in a typical shop.
list: Part number and revision, matching a drawing that is attached or already held
Drawing or model, at a stated revision, with tolerances and surface finish legible
Quantity, and ideally the quantity breaks the buyer wants priced
Material specification, including grade, condition and any certification requirement
Process requirements and any outside operations called on the print
Inspection requirements: first article, certificates of conformance, PPAP level
Required delivery date and whether it is firm or a target
Packaging, labelling and shipping instructions where they affect cost
Quote validity expectation and the buyer's terms

sections.h2: Why the drawing revision matters more than anything else on the list
paragraphs: Of everything an RFQ carries, the drawing revision is the field that causes the most expensive failures when it is wrong or missing. A quote priced against revision C and an order placed against revision D are not the same job, and the difference is usually discovered after material has been cut.

The failure is rarely anybody's fault. A customer's engineering department releases a revision and tells purchasing, and purchasing places an order without realising the supplier quoted the previous version. Both sides behaved reasonably. The only reliable protection is that the quote records which revision it priced, and that the purchase order is compared against that record before the job is released.

sections.h2: How a manufacturer should handle an inbound RFQ
paragraphs: The first decision is not how to price it but whether to price it. A shop with two estimators and forty inbound requests a week cannot properly quote all forty, so a triage step is unavoidable. Doing it deliberately — against part family, quantity band, customer history and whether the work sits inside your capability envelope — produces better outcomes than the default, which is quoting whichever request happens to be on top.

The second decision is completeness. An RFQ missing a tolerance, a material grade or a quantity should generate a question back to the buyer within the hour, not sit in a queue until an estimator opens it three days later and discovers it cannot be priced. Parking incomplete requests with a clock on the outstanding question is one of the cheapest process improvements available to a shop.

The third is the response itself, which should be a firm price, a firm lead time, a stated validity period and an explicit list of what is and is not included. And where the answer is no, a same-day decline with a reason is genuinely better for the relationship than silence. Buyers running their own clock value a fast no; they remember a week of nothing.

sections.h2: RFQ in the wider workflow
paragraphs: In an RFQ-to-Order workflow the request is the first record and everything downstream inherits from it. The quote references the RFQ. The revisions reference the quote. The acceptance locks a revision. The purchase order is matched against the locked revision. The order handed to production carries the part, revision, quantity and price that survived that match.

Treating the RFQ as a first-class record rather than as an email with attachments is what makes that chain possible. It is also what makes response time measurable, because the clock starts when the request arrives rather than when somebody remembers it exists.

sections.h2: Common mistakes
paragraphs: Treating an RFQ as a sales lead is the first. A lead is a name and an interest; an RFQ is a specification with a deadline, and a pipeline stage does not capture forty line items with drawing revisions.
Splitting a large RFQ across several quotes is the second. A ninety-line request quoted as three unrelated documents is impossible for a buyer to compare and impossible for you to revise coherently.
Not recording no-bids is the third. A declined RFQ with a reason is market data. A declined RFQ with no record is a hole in your understanding of what work you are turning away and why.

faqs.q: Is CPQ the same as quoting software?
faqs.a: Not originally. CPQ means configure, price, quote — a system that enforces valid product configurations and derives a price from them. The term has broadened in marketing usage to cover almost any quoting tool, so ask whether there is an actual configurator before treating the label as meaningful.

faqs.q: Does a job shop need CPQ?
faqs.a: Usually not. CPQ needs a product catalogue and option rules to work with, and a job shop quoting from customer drawings has neither. What a job shop needs is estimating depth: a cost buildup, quantity breaks and margin floors.

faqs.q: Can a general CRM handle manufacturing quotes?
faqs.a: It can be configured to, and plenty of manufacturers have done it. What you are buying with that route is configuration debt — a system your business designed and now maintains. The three things that consistently get under-scoped are revision chains, cost buildups and approval routing on margin.

faqs.q: What is a manufacturing CRM then?
faqs.a: A CRM whose native objects are the ones a manufacturer works with: an RFQ with line items and a drawing revision, a quote that is a cost buildup, a revision chain you can diff, an acceptance that locks a revision, and a purchase order matched against it.

faqs.q: We sell a standard machine with options plus custom handling. Which do we need?
faqs.a: You have both problems. The base machine is a configuration problem and the custom handling is an estimating problem. In practice most builders in that position need estimating depth with priced alternates rather than a full option-rule engine.

faqs.q: Do any of these replace an ERP?
faqs.a: None of them. CPQ, CRM and manufacturing CRM all stop before the shop floor. Scheduling, routings, inventory, work in process and job costing against actuals belong to an ERP, and a vendor claiming to cover both halves is usually selling an ERP under a different name.

faqs.q: What is the single question that separates the categories?
faqs.a: Does your price come from a configuration or from an estimate? If a competent person can derive it by selecting valid options from a catalogue, that is CPQ. If somebody has to decide how the thing will be made, it is estimating and CPQ has nothing to offer.

terms.title: CPQ vs CRM: what is the difference?
terms.h1: CPQ vs CRM: what is the difference?
terms.description: CPQ configures a product and prices it from rules; CRM holds the customer relationship and the deal. What each does, and what a manufacturing CRM adds.
terms.answer: CPQ software configures a product from option rules and prices the result; CRM software holds the customer, the conversation and the deal. A job shop quoting from customer drawings has no catalogue to configure, which is why KanchanFlow is a manufacturing RFQ-to-Order CRM with a real cost buildup rather than either one.

sections.h2: What CPQ actually does
paragraphs: CPQ stands for configure, price, quote. It exists to solve a specific problem: a company sells a product with many valid configurations, the combinations are governed by rules, and salespeople get them wrong. A CPQ system holds the option model, enforces which choices are compatible, derives a price from the resulting configuration and generates a quote document.

The classic examples are enterprise software licensing, telecoms bundles, industrial equipment with option packages, and vehicles. In each case there is a catalogue, there are rules, and there is a correct price for any valid combination. CPQ is genuinely valuable there and it saves companies a great deal of money in mispriced deals.

sections.h2: What CRM actually does
paragraphs: CRM software holds the customer relationship: the accounts, the contacts, the conversations, the open opportunities and the activity history. Its organising object is the deal, and its native question is where each deal sits and what happens next.

A general CRM is deliberately industry-agnostic, which is its strength and its limitation. It will hold anything you tell it to hold, and it knows nothing in particular about any of it. A quote in a general CRM is typically a document with line items and a total, not a cost buildup with material yields, setup minutes and outside-service vendor quotes.

sections.h2: Why a job shop fits neither category cleanly
paragraphs: A job shop does not have a product catalogue. It has a print that arrived this morning for a part nobody has made before. There is nothing to configure, no option rules to enforce, and no price to derive from a configuration — the price comes from an estimator deciding how the part will be made on your machines with your people.

So CPQ, in its pure form, has nothing to work with. And a general CRM has nowhere to put the four cost columns, the quantity breaks, the drawing revision, the outside-service vendor quote and the revision chain that a manufacturing quote actually needs.

This is why so many shops end up with a CRM that holds the customer and a spreadsheet that holds the quote. The arrangement is not stupid; it is a rational response to two products that each solve half the problem. It fails at the seam — the quote leaves as a PDF and stops being a record, so there is no revision history, no follow-up cadence and no way to prove what Rev 2 said.

sections.h2: The distinction that actually decides it
paragraphs: Ask one question: does your price come from a configuration or from an estimate?

If a competent person can derive the price by selecting valid options from a catalogue, you have a configuration problem and CPQ is the right category. If the price requires somebody to decide how the thing will be made — what material to buy, how it will be held, how many setups, which operations are bought out — you have an estimating problem and CPQ has nothing to offer you.

Manufacturers sometimes have both. An equipment builder with a standard machine and an option list has a configuration problem for the base machine and an estimating problem for the custom handling that goes around it. In that case the honest answer is that you need estimating depth with alternates and options, not a full option-rule engine.

sections.h2: What a manufacturing CRM adds
paragraphs: A manufacturing CRM is a CRM whose native objects are the ones a manufacturer works with. The RFQ is a record with line items, materials, processes and a drawing revision. The quote is a cost buildup rather than a document template. Revisions form a chain you can diff. Acceptance locks a revision. The purchase order is matched against what was accepted, and the confirmed order is handed to production.

It does not configure a product, so it is not CPQ. It does not schedule or cost a job on the floor, so it is not an ERP. What it does is hold the customer-facing half of a manufacturing business in a form that matches how that half actually works.

sections.h2: How to choose between the three
paragraphs: Buy CPQ if you sell configurable products from a catalogue and your salespeople produce invalid or mispriced configurations. That is a real and expensive problem and CPQ solves it directly.
Buy a general CRM if your requirement is genuinely relationship and pipeline management, your quoting is simple, and you have someone in-house who will own the configuration if you need to extend it.

Buy a manufacturing CRM if your work arrives as customer drawings, your quoting needs a cost buildup, and you argue with buyers about what a previous revision said. And in all three cases, keep your ERP — none of these categories runs a shop floor, and any vendor suggesting otherwise is selling you an ERP under a different name.

sections.h2: A note on terminology drift
paragraphs: The word CPQ has broadened in marketing usage to mean almost any quoting software, which makes the category label less useful than it was. Several products sold as manufacturing CPQ have no configurator at all and are cost-buildup quoting tools, which is a perfectly good thing to be but is not what CPQ originally meant.

When evaluating, ignore the label and ask a concrete question: show me how you price a part I send you as a drawing, with no catalogue entry, three operations and one outside process. The answer separates the categories faster than any feature comparison.

releases.title: GSTIN validation moves to live registry lookup
releases.body: GSTIN validation on customer and vendor records now performs a live registry lookup instead of a format check. The returned registered legal name, trade name, state code, registration type and current status are written onto the party with a last-checked timestamp, and a mismatch against the name you typed is flagged. The state code feeds place-of-supply logic on every document raised for that party, so a wrong registration is caught before it produces a run of wrongly taxed invoices.

releases.title: Orders module: Quote-as-Order, staged billing and partial dispatch
releases.body: The orders module is live on every tier. An accepted quote revision converts to an order carrying its own line structure, and each line tracks ordered, dispatched and invoiced quantities independently so partial dispatch is the normal case rather than an exception. Staged billing supports advance, on-dispatch and milestone splits. The order stays open until all three quantities agree on every line, and keeps a permanent link back to the exact quote revision the customer accepted.

releases.title: Credit and debit notes reference their parent invoice
releases.body: Credit and debit notes are now raised against a specific invoice rather than as free-standing documents. The note appears on both records, carries the parent's tax treatment, and reconciles into the same return period. Issued invoices are no longer editable — corrections go through a note, which is what keeps the trail defensible when a customer's accounts team queries a document a year later.

releases.title: Customer credit limits block dispatch before goods leave
releases.body: A credit limit set on a customer is now checked when a dispatch is recorded, not at month end. When outstanding balance plus the value of the pending dispatch crosses the limit, the order flags before anything ships. Users with the right permission can override, and the override is written to the order with a name, a timestamp and the balance at the time of the decision.

releases.title: WhatsApp broadcasts with segmented lists and delivery reporting
releases.body: The WhatsApp Business Hub can now send an approved template to a filtered customer or dealer list as a broadcast, with delivery, read and reply counts reported back against the broadcast record. Replies thread onto the individual customer rather than into the broadcast, so a price-revision announcement that starts eleven conversations produces eleven threads on eleven accounts.

releases.title: QuickBooks connector for invoices, credit notes and payments
releases.body: The QuickBooks connector is live, joining Tally and Zoho Books. Invoices, credit notes, debit notes and recorded payments push across, with the customer matched on your chosen identifier. Starter selects one connector; Professional and Enterprise include all three. This closes the gap where the sales desk could see what was owed but the books of account had to be updated by hand.

releases.title: US tax: line-level taxability and exemption certificate expiry
releases.body: US sales tax is now resolved per line rather than per document, so an invoice can carry a taxable part line, an exempt line and freight treated according to the destination state's own rule. Resale and manufacturing exemption certificates on the customer record now carry an expiry date; an expired certificate stops applying and flags on the account rather than silently continuing to exempt.

releases.title: Locked FX rates on quotes, orders and invoices
releases.body: The exchange rate on a multi-currency quote is now captured at the moment you price it and carried to the order and invoice created from it. Rates no longer drift between quoting and invoicing. Re-rating is an explicit action that creates a new revision, so a rate change is something the customer can see rather than something they discover on the invoice.

releases.title: e-Invoice IRN cancellation inside the statutory window
releases.body: A registered invoice can now be cancelled from the invoice record with a reason code, inside the statutory window, without a portal login. The cancellation, its reason and its timestamp are stored on the invoice and the document is marked cancelled rather than deleted. Registration failures now show the portal's rejection reason against the failing field, and the invoice stays editable for resubmission.

releases.title: Native iOS and Android app: approvals, visits and customer lookup
releases.body: The native mobile app is live on the App Store and Google Play, included on every tier and every seat. It covers customer and quote lookup, order and dispatch status, GPS visit check-in, and the approval queue with quoted price, cost and resulting margin on each request. Screens are built for a phone used with gloves in daylight, and tolerate the intermittent connectivity you get inside a steel building.

releases.title: IndiaMART enquiries de-duplicate against existing accounts
releases.body: IndiaMART enquiries now match against existing contacts and accounts on phone number and company name before a lead is created. A repeat buyer attaches to their existing record with the new enquiry on the timeline instead of creating a second account. Assignment rules can route on the enquired product or category, so a lead has an owner from the moment it exists.

releases.title: Quote share links replace email attachments
releases.body: Quotes now send as a browser share link rather than a PDF attachment. The buyer opens the quote without an account, sees the line items and every attached drawing, and can accept from the link. The quote record shows first-open time, most recent open and view count. Attachments no longer bounce off a customer's mail filter, and a 6 MB drawing set is no longer a delivery problem.

releases.title: Aadhaar eSign acceptance binds to a specific quote revision
releases.body: Quote acceptance via Aadhaar eSign now attaches the signed document, signer name, timestamp and provider transaction reference to the exact revision that was signed. A later revision starts unsigned, so a signature never carries silently across a price change. The signed document travels to the order created from the accepted revision and stays with it for the life of the job.

releases.title: Approval-first AI agents: RFQ extraction and quote follow-up
releases.body: The first two AI agents are live on every tier. The RFQ Agent turns an enquiry email into a structured RFQ at two credits per extract; the Quote Follow-Up Agent drafts the chase message at one credit. Both stop for human approval before anything is created or sent, and each extracted field is displayed against the source text it came from so checking the work takes seconds rather than a re-read.

You deliver KanchanFlow onboarding, data migration from spreadsheets and legacy CRMs, ERP integration on the order-handoff boundary, and role-based training for estimators, inside sales and the owner.

types.body: Your ERP handles the shop floor, the routing, the inventory and the general ledger. It does not handle the twenty-two RFQs sitting in an estimator's inbox, the Rev 4 quote nobody followed up on, or the dealer who has gone quiet. KanchanFlow becomes the CRM layer in front of the ERP you already sell, and the handoff point is the accepted quote.

Order handoff into the ERP at quote acceptance — we do not try to own routing, BOM or MRP
A clean anti-position that avoids channel conflict with your ERP vendor
Co-sell motion into your installed base rather than a cold-outbound program

types.who: Trade associations such as NAM and AMT, US MEP centers, industrial distributors and marketplace channels.
types.body: You reach thousands of small and mid-size manufacturers who are still quoting from spreadsheets. A channel arrangement gives your members or customers a manufacturing-specific CRM at a price a 12-person shop can approve, with member-rate onboarding and a named contact on our side.
delivers: Member or customer offers, negotiated per agreement rather than published here
Joint webinars and workshop content written for estimators, not for software buyers
Co-branded RFQ and quoting educational material your members can actually use
Event booth co-op at trade shows where your members already gather
types.economics: Referral share on the subscription, or a flat channel arrangement where a revenue share is not appropriate for your organization type.

whyPartner.title: Real product depth, not a thin CRM shell
whyPartner.body: WhatsApp Business API with template management, marketplace lead capture including IndiaMART, accounting connectors for Tally, Zoho Books and QuickBooks, payments through Razorpay and Stripe, thirteen AI agents that always route through human approval before anything leaves the building, and a native mobile app built for the shop floor. You are not selling a contact database with a manufacturing skin on it.

whyPartner.title: Land-and-expand pricing a shop owner signs off in one meeting
whyPartner.body: $39 per user per month on Starter with a three-user minimum, $49 on Professional. A first landing is a few hundred dollars a year, not a capital request. That matters when your buyer is a 55-year-old owner who has already been burned by a six-figure system that took eighteen months and never got used.

whyPartner.title: Sub-6-week standard implementation
whyPartner.body: Twelve pre-built manufacturing templates cover the common verticals, so a standard implementation runs under six weeks rather than the two-quarter slog an ERP module takes. Faster delivery means more engagements per consultant per year, and a reference you can name sooner.

whyPartner.title: Recurring revenue share, not a one-time bounty
whyPartner.body: Referral share is paid on year-one subscription revenue and again on every renewal, at the rate your tier earns. The renewal rate is deliberately close to the year-one rate because the partner who keeps a customer live is worth more to us than the partner who only made the introduction.

whyPartner.title: Priority technical access
whyPartner.body: MCP server SDK, REST API with a published rate limit, a maintained Postman collection, webhook documentation and a partner sandbox workspace that is separate from your customers' production data. Registered partners get sandbox access on approval, before the first deal closes.

whyPartner.title: Co-marketing that produces artifacts you can reuse
whyPartner.body: Joint case studies with quantified before-and-after numbers, joint webinars to your list and ours, and a trade-show booth split at Gold and above. Every asset carries your firm's name, not just ours.

tiers.benefits: Directory listing, technical docs, sandbox access, 15% year 1 / 10% renewal referral share

tiers.benefits: Above, plus 20% / 15%, quarterly partner webinar, priority support SLA

tiers.requirements: 15 paying customers + 2 certified consultants + 1 published case study
tiers.benefits: Above, plus 25% / 18%, dedicated partner success manager, co-marketing budget, trade-show booth co-op

tiers.requirements: 40+ paying customers + 4 certified consultants + verified regional coverage
tiers.benefits: Above, plus 30% / 20%, joint go-to-market plan, exclusive geographic territories, roadmap input

guardrails.title: No territory exclusivity below Platinum
guardrails.body: Exclusive geographic territory is a Platinum benefit only, and only under a signed contract that names the territory and the performance floor that keeps it. Nobody below Platinum has an exclusive anything, and we will say so plainly to any customer who asks.

guardrails.title: No case study without customer approval and real numbers
guardrails.body: We do not publish a case study until the named customer has approved the text in writing and the before-and-after numbers are quantified. No anonymous composites, no 'a leading fabricator', no percentage improvements without a stated baseline.

guardrails.title: Deal registration is first-registered, first-served, 30-day validity
guardrails.body: The first partner to register an opportunity holds it for 30 days. If it has not progressed in 30 days it reopens. This is how we prevent channel conflict, and it applies to us too: our own sales team respects an active registration.

guardrails.title: Certification proves knowledge, not endorsement
guardrails.body: A certified consultant has passed our exam and delivered a sandbox project. That is a statement about product knowledge. It is not a warranty of the firm's work, a guarantee of outcomes, or an endorsement by Soor LLC of anything else that firm sells.

guardrails.title: No firms with exclusive commitments to directly competing vendors
guardrails.body: If your firm is under an exclusivity agreement with a directly competing manufacturing CRM, we will decline the application. Reselling an ERP is not competing — being contractually bound to a rival CRM is. Tell us upfront; we would rather decline at application than unwind it later.

certificationTracks.name: KanchanFlow Certified Implementer
certificationTracks.prerequisite: None. Open to any employee of an approved Registered partner.
certificationTracks.assessment: 80-question product exam (pass mark 80%) plus a delivered sandbox project reviewed by our team against a published rubric.
certificationTracks.summary: The base credential. Twenty hours of online course, an exam, and one sandbox project delivered end to end. It certifies that you can configure a workspace, migrate a shop off spreadsheets and hand a live system to an estimator without our help.

modules.name: Manufacturing sales fundamentals for implementers
modules.body: How a job shop actually gets from an inbound RFQ to a purchase order: estimator workload, the quote-follow-up gap, why shops lose work to no-decision rather than to a competitor, and where a CRM helps versus where it gets in the way.

modules.name: Platform architecture and the anti-position
modules.body: Objects, relationships and permissions. What KanchanFlow owns (RFQ, quote, revision, order handoff, dealer, territory) and what it deliberately does not (ERP, MRP, CAD, BOM, advanced CPQ) — so you scope engagements honestly.

modules.name: RFQ intake and lead source configuration
modules.body: Email intake and AI extraction, marketplace and web-form capture, manual entry for phone RFQs, deduplication rules, and qualification scoring thresholds tuned to the shop's real win rate.

modules.name: Quoting, cost buildup and revision control
modules.body: The 4-column cost buildup, margin guardrails, quantity breaks, alternate variants, the quote diff view, and unlimited revision history — including how to explain Rev 0 to Rev 7 traceability to an owner who has only ever used a spreadsheet.

modules.name: Approval engine and workflow automation
modules.body: Approval rules by margin, value and customer, escalation paths, notification design that does not train people to ignore alerts, and the automation patterns that survive contact with a busy shop.

modules.name: Data migration and workspace setup
modules.body: Field mapping from spreadsheets and legacy CRM exports, deduplication and cleanup, staged import, the go-live cutover checklist, and rollback if the cutover goes wrong.

modules.name: Integrations and order handoff
modules.body: REST API basics, webhook design, the accounting connectors (Tally, Zoho Books, QuickBooks), payments (Razorpay, Stripe), and building the ERP order-handoff boundary at quote acceptance.

modules.name: Training, adoption and the 30-day check
modules.body: Role-based training for owner, estimator, inside sales and shop-floor mobile users; the adoption metrics that predict churn; and running the 30-day post-go-live review so problems surface while they are still cheap.

modules.name: Sandbox project and exam
modules.body: Project brief walkthrough, the review rubric, exam format and retake policy. The sandbox project is delivered in your own partner sandbox and reviewed against the same rubric for every candidate.

certificationTracks.name: KanchanFlow Certified Manufacturing Consultant
certificationTracks.assessment: Scenario-based exam with two written case responses, graded by a member of our team rather than auto-marked.
certificationTracks.summary: A further ten hours on top of the Implementer credential, covering the advanced surface: RFQ workflow design, CPQ boundaries, dealer and distributor management, e-invoicing and the immutable audit trail. This is the credential that counts toward Silver, Gold and Platinum tier requirements.

modules.name: Advanced RFQ workflow design
modules.body: Designing intake and triage for a shop taking 60+ RFQs a week: routing by commodity and machine group, qualification scoring calibration, no-quote discipline, and measuring estimator capacity honestly.

modules.name: CPQ boundaries and cost model design
modules.body: Building a defensible cost model — material, labor, outside process, overhead — with margin guardrails and quantity breaks, and knowing exactly where our 4-column buildup stops and a real CPQ or ERP costing engine has to start.

modules.name: Dealer and distributor management
modules.body: The 5-level dealer hierarchy, the 7-level territory tree, dealer portal rollout, dealer health scoring, and channel conflict rules that hold up when two dealers claim the same account.

modules.name: E-invoicing and India regulatory features
modules.body: GST, GSTIN validation, HSN, e-Invoice IRN generation and the MSMED Section 43B(h) tracker — scoped for USA manufacturers with India operations, India-based contract customers, or export exposure to India. Included on every tier, never an upsell.

modules.name: Immutable audit trail and compliance engagements
modules.body: The immutable audit log, what it does and does not prove, and how to position it for ITAR, PPAP, USMCA and Buy America work — including the sentence you must be able to say out loud: KanchanFlow is the CRM, not the certifier.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to become a partner?
faqs.a: Nothing. There is no partner fee, no annual minimum purchase and no required inventory. The certification course, the exam, the sandbox and the technical resources are included with an approved partner agreement. We make money when your customer pays a subscription, which is the only arrangement that keeps our incentives pointed the same direction as yours.

faqs.q: How does the referral share actually get paid?
faqs.a: Monthly in arrears, once the customer's invoice is settled. Registered earns 15% of year-one subscription revenue and 10% on every renewal; Silver 20% / 15%; Gold 25% / 18%; Platinum 30% / 20%. The rate applies to subscription revenue only — not to add-ons billed at cost, WhatsApp message pass-through, or your own implementation fees, which are yours entirely.

faqs.q: Will KanchanFlow sell directly into my accounts?
faqs.a: Not into a registered one. Deal registration is first-registered, first-served with 30-day validity, and our sales team sees the same registration you do. Outside a registration we do sell direct — we are honest about that rather than promising a channel-only motion we would not keep.

faqs.q: Do I get an exclusive territory?
faqs.a: Only at Platinum, and only under a signed contract that names the territory and the performance floor required to keep it. Below Platinum nobody holds an exclusive, and we will tell any customer who asks exactly that.

faqs.q: I already resell an ERP. Is this a conflict?
faqs.a: No — it is the point. KanchanFlow sits in front of the ERP and hands off at quote acceptance. We do not do routing, MRP, BOM management, inventory or the general ledger, so there is nothing for your ERP vendor to object to. What we will decline is a firm under an exclusivity agreement with a directly competing manufacturing CRM.

faqs.q: How long does an implementation take?
faqs.a: Under six weeks for a standard engagement using the pre-built manufacturing templates: discovery and process mapping, workspace configuration, data migration, integration and order handoff, training, then a 30-day adoption check. Multi-entity, ERP-heavy or dealer-channel engagements run longer, and we would rather you scope that honestly than promise six weeks and miss.

faqs.q: How many partners do you have today?
faqs.a: None. The program opened with the Wave 1 launch and the directory is genuinely empty. We could have filled it with logos nobody signed off on; we would rather you see an empty page and know that every listing on it later is real.
